questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman comes to the physician's office complaining of enlarged finger and shoe size. Her fingers and shoe size have constantly increased for the last 6 months. The patient also complains that he has a dough-like consistency in her extremities. Moreover, she is also experiencing hyperhidrosis and skin tags. The vital signs are normal. On physical examination, the jaw size looks larger than her face. Which of the following is a hallmark feature of this condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 36-year-old woman comes to the physician's office complaining of enlarged finger and shoe size. Her fingers and shoe size have constantly increased for the last 6 months. The patient also complains that he has a dough-like consistency in her extremities. Moreover, she is also experiencing hyperhidrosis and skin tags. The vital signs are normal. On physical examination, the jaw size looks larger than her face. Which of the following is a hallmark feature of this condition?

options.label: B
options.text: Growth of the mandible and soft tissues of the face

options.label: C
options.text: Growth of the hands and feet

options.label: D
options.text: Growth of the thorax and abdomen

questions.answerText: Growth of the mandible and soft tissues of the face
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Growth of the mandible and soft tissues of the face: The patient with the presenting complaints of hyperhidrosis, skin tags, and increased shoe and finger size has most likely the diagnosis with acromegaly. Acromegaly or gigantism occur due to the hypersecretion of the growth hormone. When growth hormone hypersecretion occurs before the fusion of long bone, then gigantism occurs. When the hormone hypersecretion occurs after the fusion of epiphysis, causing large extremities and characteristic faces, it causes acromegaly. The hallmark feature of acromegaly is the overgrowth of bones and soft tissues, particularly in the face and extremities. This leads to a number of characteristic physical features, including an enlarged jaw (prognathism), thickening of the skin, and enlargement of the hands and feet. However, long bone growth is not affected in acromegaly because the growth plates have already fused in adults. Incorrect Options: Option A - Growth of long bones: Growth of long bones is incorrect because, as mentioned earlier, the growth plates in bones have already fused in adults and therefore, acromegaly does not affect long bone growth. Option C - Growth of the hands and feet: Growth of the hands and feet is partially correct because acromegaly does lead to enlargement of the hands and feet due to overgrowth of soft tissues, but not the bones themselves. Option D - Growth of the thorax and abdomen: Growth of the thorax and abdomen is also partially correct because acromegaly can cause enlargement of the organs in the thorax and abdomen, such as the heart and liver, but not the bones themselves. @Neet_pg_bot

He takes levothyroxine 100mcg by mouth daily, prednisone 5 mg by mouth daily, and is on a testosterone patch. He has not been able to take this oral medication for two days. Patient is febrile at 100.8 degrees Fahrenheit, heart rate is 88 beats/min, blood pressure is 101/77mmHg and saturating well at 98% on RA. Physical exam and labs are unremarkable, except that he tests positive for influenza. What is the best plan for this patient?

questions.stem: A 56-year-old female is admitted to the hospital due to palpitations and dyspnea. The patient had 2 episodes of loss of consciousness in the past month and complains of occasional episodes of her heart ‘skipping a beat’. Past medical history is significant for treatment-resistant depression, hypertension and type II diabetes mellitus. ECG tracing is shown below. Which of the following medications is the most likely cause of this patient’s condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 56-year-old female is admitted to the hospital due to palpitations and dyspnea. The patient had 2 episodes of loss of consciousness in the past month and complains of occasional episodes of her heart ‘skipping a beat’. Past medical history is significant for treatment-resistant depression, hypertension and type II diabetes mellitus. ECG tracing is shown below. Which of the following medications is the most likely cause of this patient’s condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option C- Amitriptyline: This patient’s clinical presentation and ECG findings suggest torsades de pointes . Long QT interval is the inciting factor that predisposes to torsades de pointes. ECG shows irregular QRS complexes of varying amplitude. This patient with treatment-resistant depression is most likely taking amitriptyline which causes the prolongation of QT interval. Other common causes of QT interval prolongation include: Antiarrhythmic (e.g. Class IA and IC) Antibiotics (e.g. macrolides) Antipsychotics (e.g. haloperidol) Antiemetics (e.g. ondansetron) Hypocalcemia Hypomagnesemia Hypokalemia Treatment options include: IV magnesium sulfate Atrial pacing IV isoprenaline Implantable defibrillator (QT > 500 msec) After the patient is stabilized, underlying causes should be rectified. Incorrect Options: Option A- Metformin: Metformin is the oral drug of choice in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (DM) and works by inhibiting hepatic glucose production. Metformin doesn’t cause QT interval prolongation. Important side effects include: Vitamin B 12 deficiency Lactic acidosis Metformin should be used cautiously in patients with renal and hepatic dysfunction. Option B- Lisinopril: Lisinopril is an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor (ACE inhibitor). It is commonly used as the drug of choice in patients with hypertension. Lisinopril doesn’t cause QT interval prolongation. Important side effects include: Hypotension Dry cough Angioedema Hyperkalemia Renal dysfunction Option D- Verapamil: Verapamil is a calcium channel blocker which usually affects the PR interval, so it would not cause QT interval prolongation. Common side effects include: Bradycardia Heart block Constipation Hypotension Verapamil is used for rate control in patients with atrial fibrillation. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 66-year-old male is brought to the emergency room with a complaint of acute onset of severe shortness of breath. He had a history of myocardial infarction 3 weeks ago. On examination, a new murmur of mitral regurgitation is appreciated, and S1 and S2 are normal. Blood pressure 110/80 mmHg. Pulmonary auscultation shows fine end-inspiratory basilar crackles in both lungs. Jugular pulsation is not evident. Chest X-ray is ordered and is shown below; which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 66-year-old male is brought to the emergency room with a complaint of acute onset of severe shortness of breath. He had a history of myocardial infarction 3 weeks ago. On examination, a new murmur of mitral regurgitation is appreciated, and S1 and S2 are normal. Blood pressure 110/80 mmHg. Pulmonary auscultation shows fine end-inspiratory basilar crackles in both lungs. Jugular pulsation is not evident. Chest X-ray is ordered and is shown below; which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option A- Congestive cardiac failure: The patient's presentation is consistent with acute pulmonary oedema due to congestive cardiac failure. Congestive heart failure is the inability of the heart to pump enough blood due to pathological changes in the myocardium to meet the metabolic requirements of the body. There are many causes of congestive cardiac failure; however, the most common and important are myocardial infarction, hypertension and diabetes mellitus. The patient presents with shortness of breath due to pulmonary congestion caused by impaired contractility of the heart leading to fluid build-up in the lungs. Orthopnoea (shortness of breath when lying flat) and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea (patient wakes up due to shortness of breath due to increased venous return). A new murmur of mitral regurgitation due to papillary muscle is the precipitating cause. On pulmonary auscultation, fine end-inspiratory basilar crackles in both lungs are highly characteristic. Incorrect Options: Option B- Pulmonary embolism: Pulmonary embolism also presents with sudden onset shortness of breath. However, the patient has thromboembolic risk factors such as recent surgery, prolonged immobilization, previously documented deep venous thrombosis, active cancer, paralysis, calf swelling, and varicose veins. Moreover, a chest X-ray shows Hampton Hump (a peripheral wedge-shaped opacity at the peripheral lung parenchyma caused by pulmonary infarction). Option C- Tension pneumothorax: Tension pneumothorax also presents with sudden severe shortness of breath. The presence of tracheal deviation and hyper resonant percussion with hemodynamic instability and the absence of broncho vascular markings on chest X-ray is suggestive of tension pneumothorax. It is a life-threatening condition in which the damaged tissue acts as a one-way valve in which the air enters the pleural cavity but cannot escape naturally, resulting in increased pressure into the pleural space, compressing the lung and mediastinum to the opposite side. Mediastinal deviation causes compression of the veins manifesting as jugular venous distension resulting in impaired venous return to the heart, manifesting as hemodynamic collapse (low blood pressure and tachycardia). Option D- Cardiac tamponade: Cardiac tamponade is an emergency caused by increased pericardial pressure due to pericardial effusion, which compresses the right ventricle. It is characterized by Beck’s triad of elevated jugular pulsation, hypotension, and muffled heart sounds. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 64-year-old asthmatic female with dementia was found lying on the floor at home. She was lethargic, her heart rate was 52 beats per minute, and her blood pressure was 80/50 mmHg. Her work of breathing was mildly increased, and a lung exam revealed diffuse wheezes bilaterally. Next to her was an empty bottle of propranolol. Presuming that her condition was due to a beta blocker overdose, what is the mechanism of action of the reversal agent?
questions.stemHtml: A 64-year-old asthmatic female with dementia was found lying on the floor at home. She was lethargic, her heart rate was 52 beats per minute, and her blood pressure was 80/50 mmHg. Her work of breathing was mildly increased, and a lung exam revealed diffuse wheezes bilaterally. Next to her was an empty bottle of propranolol. Presuming that her condition was due to a beta blocker overdose, what is the mechanism of action of the reversal agent?

options.label: A
options.text: Adsorption of the drug in the gastrointestinal tract

options.label: B
options.text: Serum alkalization to allow acid dissociation and excretion

options.label: D
options.text: An increase in cyclic AMP, elevating intracellular calcium available for depolarization

questions.answerText: An increase in cyclic AMP, elevating intracellular calcium available for depolarization
questions.solution: Correct Option D - An increase in cyclic AMP, elevating intracellular calcium available for depolarization: Beta-blocker overdose can be lethal, presenting with cardiogenic shock and ventricular arrhythmias . Signs and symptoms of toxicity typically occur within 2-6 hours of ingestion. Non-cardiac effects include altered mental status, seizures, hypoglycemia, and wheezing . Beta-blockers may cause bronchoconstriction via blockade of bronchial beta-2 receptors, worsening symptoms in asthmatic patients. This is particularly true for non-selective beta blockers such as propranolol. Cardioselective beta blockers (such as atenolol, metoprolol, and bisoprolol, among others) preferentially block cardiac beta-1 receptors and have less of an effect on the airways. Glucagon is a first-line reversal agent for beta-blocker overdose and works by activating adenylate cyclase in a manner independent of beta receptors. This increases the production of cyclic AMP. Increased cAMP raises intracellular calcium, improving muscle contractility. It should be noted that although glucagon is often considered for initial use in beta blocker overdose, high-quality data confirming its effectiveness are limited. Incorrect Options: Option A - Adsorption of the drug in the gastrointestinal tract : Activated charcoal adsorbs ingested substances and prevents absorption from the gastrointestinal tract. It is most useful when the ingestion is recent. Option B - Serum alkalization to allow acid dissociation and excretion : In cases of salicylate poisoning, alkalization of the serum and urine with sodium bicarbonate is useful in dissociating salicylic acid into hydrogen and salicylate, which is then excreted in urine. Option C - Restoration of hepatic glutathione : This mechanism characterizes the action of N-acetylcysteine, which is used for acetaminophen toxicity. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 25-year-old male presents with recurring episodes of wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. These symptoms are only triggered in certain situations, which the patient can’t point out. He also reports coughing and difficulty breathing during exercise. His medical history is significant for eczema. On physical examination, the patient has diffuse wheezing and prolonged expiration. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 25-year-old male presents with recurring episodes of wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. These symptoms are only triggered in certain situations, which the patient can’t point out. He also reports coughing and difficulty breathing during exercise. His medical history is significant for eczema. On physical examination, the patient has diffuse wheezing and prolonged expiration. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Allergic asthma: Allergic asthma is the most common form of asthma, accounting for around 50-60% of all asthma cases. It is an immunoglobulin E (Ig E)-mediated hypersensitivity reaction to various allergens, including house dust mites, pollen, animal dander, and moulds. In allergic asthma, allergens are inhaled and processed by antigen-presenting cells (APCs) in the airways. These APCs then present allergen peptides to T-helper 2 (Th2) cells, which produce interleukins, such as IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 . These interleukins activate eosinophils, which release inflammatory mediators such as leukotrienes and prostaglandins, causing bronchial smooth muscle contraction, airway oedema, and mucus production. In addition, Ig E antibodies produced by B cells in response to the allergens bind to mast cells and basophils, triggering the release of histamine and other inflammatory mediators. Symptoms of allergic asthma include wheezing, coughing, shortness of breath, and chest tightness, which occur in response to exposure to allergens. Incorrect Options: Option B - Occupational asthma: Occupational asthma is caused by exposure to irritants or allergens in the workplace. It is estimated to account for approximately 5-15% of adult asthma cases. While the patient's symptoms could potentially be caused by occupational asthma, the fact that she has a history of allergies makes allergic asthma a more likely diagnosis. Option C - Exercise-induced asthma: Exercise-induced asthma (EIA) is a type of asthma that is triggered by physical exertion. It is estimated to affect approximately 90% of individuals with asthma. However, in this scenario, the patient's symptoms are not necessarily related to physical exertion, so EIA is less likely to be the cause of her symptoms. Option D - Non-allergic asthma: Non-allergic asthma, also known as intrinsic asthma , is asthma that is not caused by an allergic response. It is estimated to account for approximately 30-40% of adult asthma cases. However, the patient's history of allergies makes allergic asthma a more likely diagnosis than non-allergic asthma. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following mechanisms best describes the therapeutic action of Nusinersen in the treatment of Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA)?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following mechanisms best describes the therapeutic action of Nusinersen in the treatment of Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA)?

options.label: A
options.text: Nusinersen promotes the production of dystrophin in motor neurons.

options.label: B
options.text: Nusinersen increases the expression of SMN protein by enhancing transcription.

options.label: C
options.text: Nusinersen inhibits the fusion of muscle cells, preventing muscle wasting.

options.label: D
options.text: Nusinersen directly stimulates muscle growth and development.

questions.answerText: Nusinersen increases the expression of SMN protein by enhancing transcription.
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Nusinersen increases the expression of SMN protein by enhancing transcription: Nusinersen is an FDA-approved treatment for Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA), a genetic disorder characterized by the deficiency of the survival motor neuron (SMN) protein. Nusinersen works by modifying SMN2 pre-mRNA splicing to increase the production of functional SMN protein. This is achieved by enhancing transcription, leading to the inclusion of exon 7 in SMN2 mRNA, which ultimately results in the production of a fully functional SMN protein. This therapeutic approach aims to compensate for the reduced or non-functional SMN protein in SMA patients. Incorrect Options: Option A - Nusinersen promotes the production of dystrophin in motor neurons: Nusinersen does not promote the production of dystrophin. Dystrophin is associated with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, not SMA. Option C - Nusinersen inhibits the fusion of muscle cells, preventing muscle wasting: Nusinersen does not inhibit the fusion of muscle cells. The pathology of SMA primarily involves the loss of motor neurons, leading to muscle weakness and wasting, rather than aberrant muscle cell fusion. Option D - Nusinersen directly stimulates muscle growth and development: Nusinersen does not directly stimulate muscle growth and development. Its primary mode of action is at the level of RNA splicing to increase SMN protein production. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C- Hypokalemia: This patient has a history of Crohn's disease (CD). CD is an inflammatory bowel disease. One of the predominant manifestations of CD is diarrhoea. Protracted diarrhoea is known to cause hypokalemia due to the ineffective absorption of solutes by the intestinal epithelium. Diarrhoea in CD is due to the inflammation of the gut wall. Long-term hypokalemia is known to cause NDI , but the mechanism is poorly understood. There is some evidence to suggest that it causes the downregulation of aquaporin channels in the distal nephron. Incorrect Options: Option A- Urinary tract infection: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are likely to present with excessive urination. Also, the increased frequency of urination accompanies other lower urinary tract symptoms such as dysuria and urgency. A urinalysis in patients with a UTI will likely show at least 8-10 WBCs/hpf. UTIs are generally unlikely to cause electrolyte imbalances and changes in urine osmolality. Option B- Colovesical fistula: Colovesical fistulas are abnormal tracts formed between the colonic and bladder epithelium. These occur in CD due to transmural inflammation of the colon. questions.stemHtml: A 30-year-old man arrives at the emergency department reporting palpitations, chest discomfort, and lightheadedness. An electrocardiogram (ECG) reveals regular tachycardia with normal QRS complexes. Based on these findings, what is the most probable diagnosis for this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option C- Atrioventricular nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT): The patient's symptoms and ECG findings are consistent with the diagnosis of supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), specifically AVNRT. AVNRT is a regular tachycardia with normal QRS complexes caused by a re-entry circuit involving the AV node and its right atrial input pathways. Symptoms include chest discomfort, palpitations, lightheadedness, or breathlessness. Management options include carotid sinus pressure or the Valsalva manoeuvre for acute episodes, while adenosine, verapamil, intravenous β-blockers, or flecainide can restore sinus rhythm in most cases. DC cardioversion may be necessary for severe hemodynamic compromise. Catheter ablation is the most effective therapy for recurrent SVT, with a success rate of over 90%. Prophylaxis with oral β-blockers, verapamil, or flecainide may also be used, but long-term drug therapy can create difficulties in female patients during pregnancy. Incorrect Options: Option A- Ventricular tachycardia: Ventricular tachycardia (VT) is a rapid heart rhythm originating in the ventricles , the heart's lower chambers. VT is typically defined as a run of three or more consecutive ventricular beats at a rate of 100 beats per minute or faster. The condition can be sustained or non-sustained, meaning it can last for a short or extended period. VT can occur in patients with structural heart disease, such as previous heart attacks, cardiomyopathy, or valvular heart disease , and in patients with a normal heart. Some patients may experience symptoms such as palpitations, chest discomfort, shortness of breath, or dizziness, while others may be asymptomatic. VT can be diagnosed with an electrocardiogram (ECG) and confirmed with further testing, such as a Holter monitor or electrophysiology study. The treatment of VT depends on the underlying cause and the patient's symptoms. It may involve medication, cardioversion, ablation , or an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD). VT can be a life-threatening arrhythmia , and prompt treatment is essential to prevent complications such as cardiac arrest, heart failure, or sudden death. Option B- Atrial fibrillation: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a common cardiac arrhythmia associated with risk factors such as hypertension, heart failure, and structural heart disease. Diagnosis is confirmed on ECG, which shows an irregularly irregular rhythm with no discernible P waves. AF can be classified as paroxysmal, persistent, or permanent. Management includes rate control, rhythm control, and anticoagulation therapy based on the patient's symptoms, comorbidities, and risk of thromboembolism. Complications of AF include stroke, heart failure, and increased mortality, highlighting the importance of early detection and optimal management. Option D- Atrial flutter: Atrial flutter is an abnormal heart rhythm in the heart's upper chambers (atria). It creates a circular movement in the right atrium, seen as a saw-tooth pattern on ECG. Heart rate is usually around 150 bpm but can be as high as 300 bpm. Atrial flutter can cause a 2:1, 3:1, or 4:1 block of impulses to the lower chambers (ventricles), leading to a slower heart rate. Symptoms include palpitations, shortness of breath, and fatigue. Medical treatment includes digoxin, beta-blockers, or verapamil to control heart rate. Direct current cardioversion can restore normal rhythm; catheter ablation may be recommended. Anticoagulation therapy may be necessary to prevent blood clots. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 35-year-old female presents with shortness of breath, wheezing, and chest tightness. She has a past medical history of asthma and is currently taking a short-acting beta-agonist (SABA) as needed. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old female presents with shortness of breath, wheezing, and chest tightness. She has a past medical history of asthma and is currently taking a short-acting beta-agonist (SABA) as needed. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Start inhaled corticosteroids (ICS): Asthma management involves a combination of medication and lifestyle modifications to control symptoms and prevent exacerbations. The treatment approach is individualized based on the severity of the disease, frequency and severity of symptoms, and the patient's age and comorbidities. Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS): These are the most effective anti-inflammatory medications used in the treatment of asthma. They work by reducing airway inflammation and preventing exacerbations. ICS are usually prescribed as the first-line treatment for patients with persistent asthma. Short-acting beta-agonists (SABAs): These medications act as bronchodilators and are used to provide quick relief of symptoms such as cough, wheeze, and shortness of breath. They are usually prescribed as a rescue medication for patients with intermittent asthma or as a quick-relief medication for those with persistent asthma. Long-acting beta-agonists (LABAs): These medications are also bronchodilators but have a longer duration of action compared to SABAs. They are used in combination with ICS for patients with moderate to severe persistent asthma. Leukotriene modifiers: These medications block the action of leukotrienes, which are substances that contribute to airway inflammation. They are usually prescribed as an alternative to ICS for patients with mild persistent asthma or as an add-on therapy for those with moderate to severe persistent asthma. Theophylline: This medication relaxes the smooth muscles of the airways and improves airway function. It is usually prescribed as an add-on therapy for patients with moderate to severe persistent asthma. Incorrect Options: Option A - Prescribe a long-acting beta-agonist (LABA): Adding a LABA to SABA monotherapy is not recommended as first-line therapy for asthma control. LABAs are generally used in combination with ICS to provide additional control when ICS alone is insufficient. Option C - Prescribe a leukotriene modifier: Leukotriene modifiers are not as effective as ICS and are generally reserved as alternative therapy for patients who cannot tolerate ICS or as adjunct therapy in patients already receiving ICS. Option D - Add a theophylline medication: Theophylline medications are not recommended as first-line therapy due to their narrow therapeutic index and potential for toxicity. Theophylline medications are generally reserved as alternative therapy for patients who cannot tolerate or do not respond to ICS or LABAs. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Craniopharyngioma: This patient is likely to have a craniopharyngioma, as indicated by his symptoms and the CT head findings of a suprasellar calcified cystic mass. Although panhypopituitarism is a possible presentation, it is not always easily diagnosed. questions.stem: A 58-year-old man presents to the hospital with ‘the worst headache of his life’ and is found to have a ruptured anterior communicating artery saccular aneurysm. He undergoes successful coiling of the aneurysm. On hospital day 10 he suddenly developed right gaze preference, left face and arm weakness, and left hemineglect. If the right middle cerebral artery were insonated by Transcranial Doppler what values would you expect?

He undergoes successful coiling of the aneurysm. On hospital day 10 he suddenly developed right gaze preference, left face and arm weakness, and left hemineglect. If the right middle cerebral artery were insonated by Transcranial Doppler what values would you expect?

options.label: A

options.label: B

questions.answerText: Elevated flow velocity and elevated Lindegaard ratio
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Elevated flow velocity and elevated Lindegaard ratio: Transcranial Doppler can be used to screen for subarachnoid hemorrhage-related cerebral vasospasm. In general, cerebral vasospasm results in an increase in flow velocities. Sensitivity and specificity vary depending on the thresholds used. Flow velocity >120 cm/sec in the middle cerebral arteries is commonly considered abnormal. Flow velocity >200 cm/sec in the middle cerebral artery often suggests severe vasospasm. The Lindegaard ratio (middle cerebral artery velocity/internal carotid artery velocity) can also be used to assess for cerebral vasospasm. A Lindegaard ratio of <3 is usually considered normal. A Lindegaard ratio > 6 suggests severe vasospasm. Incorrect Options: Option A - Elevated flow velocity and reduced Lindegaard ratio: This option suggests that in the context of the patient's presentation with neurological deficits after coiling of a ruptured anterior communicating artery (ACoA) aneurysm if the right middle cerebral artery (MCA) were insonated by Transcranial Doppler (TCD), the flow velocity in the MCA would be elevated. This elevation in flow velocity could be due to the presence of high-velocity turbulent blood flow caused by vasospasm, which is a common complication following subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) and aneurysm rupture. Option B - Reduced Flow Velocity and Reduced Lindegaard Ratio: In the context of a ruptured anterior communicating artery (ACoA) aneurysm, the sudden development of right gaze preference, left face and arm weakness and left hemineglect on hospital day 10 would be suggestive of a new-onset ischemic stroke. In this case, if the right middle cerebral artery (MCA) were insonated by Transcranial Doppler (TCD), the flow velocity in the MCA would likely be reduced due to the occlusion or significant stenosis of the artery supplying blood to that territory. The Lindegaard ratio (MCA velocity/internal carotid artery velocity) could also be reduced, indicating reduced flow in the MCA. Option C - Reduced Flow Velocity and Elevated Lindegaard Ratio: This combination is less likely in the context of a new-onset ischemic stroke due to a ruptured ACoA aneurysm. An elevated Lindegaard ratio is usually associated with vasospasm, which is a common complication following subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). However, vasospasm typically occurs within the first 7-10 days after the initial bleeding, not on day 10. Therefore, an elevated Lindegaard ratio is less likely to be observed on day 10 after the coiling of the aneurysm. @Neet_pg_bot

Punch biopsy shows calcification of the middle layer of arterioles, subintimal fibrosis, and thrombotic occlusion without vasculitis. The vital signs are normal. The patient has end-stage renal disease due to diabetic nephropathy .She undergoes hemodialysis two times a week. Which of the following is most likely associated with this condition?

The patient has end-stage renal disease due to diabetic nephropathy .She undergoes hemodialysis two times a week. Which of the following is most likely associated with this condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Hyperphosphatemia: This patient is diagnosed with calciphylaxis, also known as calcific uremic arteriolopathy. This condition is characterized by systemic arteriolar calcification and soft tissue calcium deposition with local ischemia and necrosis. The risk factors are end-stage renal disease, hypercalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperparathyroidism, and warfarin drug. Common manifestations are painful ulcers and soft tissue classification on imaging. It is diagnosed by skin biopsy , which shows calcification of the middle layer of arterioles, subintimal fibrosis, and thrombotic occlusion without vasculitis Management, including painkillers and wound. Optimization of dialysis is also an option. Incorrect Options: Option A - Hypermagnisimia: Magnesium inhibits extraosseous calcification , so hyper magnesium decreases the risk of this condition. Option C - Hypercalcemia: Hypercalcium is a risk factor, not hypocalcemia. Option D - Recurrent hypoglycemia: Diabetes mellitus increases the risk of calciphylaxis. The patient with end-stage renal disease may experience hypoglycemia due to decreased insulin clearance, e.g., the increased half-life of insulin. Still, hypocalcemia is not the risk factor of this condition @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 32-year-old ecologist working in a remote region is bitten by an unidentified mammal. Concerned about potential rabies exposure, the patient seeks immediate medical attention. Steller stain, known for its specificity, is most commonly employed in visualizing a distinctive feature of the rabies virus. What precise viral component does Steller stain predominantly highlight?
questions.stemHtml: A 32-year-old ecologist working in a remote region is bitten by an unidentified mammal. Concerned about potential rabies exposure, the patient seeks immediate medical attention. Steller stain, known for its specificity, is most commonly employed in visualizing a distinctive feature of the rabies virus. What precise viral component does Steller stain predominantly highlight?
questions.solution: Correct Option B- Rabies virus nucleocapsid protein: Steller stain, or Negri bodies stain, specifically highlights intracytoplasmic inclusions called Negri bodies. These bodies contain the nucleocapsid protein of the rabies virus. Identifying Negri bodies is a crucial diagnostic feature in suspected rabies cases. Incorrect Options: Option A- Rabies virus RNA genome: Steller stain does not directly target the viral RNA genome. It is designed to visualize structural components within infected cells, particularly the nucleocapsid. Option C-Rabies virus matrix glycoprotein: The matrix glycoprotein is not the primary focus of Steller stain. Negri bodies predominantly contain the nucleocapsid protein, aiding in the identification of rabies virus-infected cells. Option D- Rabies virus fusion peptide: The fusion peptide is involved in the viral entry process, but Steller stain is not designed to highlight this specific peptide. It is tailored to visualize intracytoplasmic inclusions indicative of rabies virus infection. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Fluid restriction: In this case, the patient has mild hyponatremia, and his urine is more concentrated than his blood, which is indicative of the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) in a patient with a recent head injury. Nonsevere hyponatremia associated with SIADH requires fluid restriction as the first-line management approach. Dilutional euvolemic hyponatremia caused by antidiuretic hormone can be reversed by reducing fluid intake. The reduction in fluid intake must be to a level where the excretion of free water is greater than that of free water intake. Pharmacological therapy with vasopressin receptor antagonists, such as tolvaptan, should be considered if the fluid restriction is unsuccessful in increasing serum sodium levels. Incorrect Options: Option A - Vasopressin: Vasopressin is a hormone that controls water retention in the body. It is a treatment option for diabetes insipidus, which results in excessive urine production due to insufficient ADH. Vasopressin is not suitable for treating hyponatremia caused by SIADH. Option B - Desmopressin: Desmopressin is a synthetic form of ADH that is used to treat diabetes insipidus. Like vasopressin, it would not be appropriate for treating SIADH. Increasing antidiuretic hormone in this man would make his hyponatremia worse. Option D - Demeclocycline: Demeclocycline is an antibiotic drug that can be used to treat SIADH (Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion). It works by blocking the action of ADH (antidiuretic hormone) which is responsible for water retention in the body. It is not recommended as a first-line treatment for asymptomatic hyponatremia caused by SIADH. It is usually reserved for severe cases of hyponatremia that are resistant to fluid restriction and other therapies. @Neet_pg_bot

Which of the following would be part of an appropriate response to the student?
questions.stemHtml: A 75-year-old retired physician, diagnosed with Parkinson's disease (PD) at age 60, is brought in for a clinic visit due to his wife’s concern about changes in his thinking and behavior. You opt to go forward with screening him for cognitive dysfunction via a Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) as opposed to a Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE). The medical student working with you has only used the MMSE and has never heard of the MoCA and questions your choice in pursuing the MoCA over the MMSE. Which of the following would be part of an appropriate response to the student?

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C

questions.answerText: The MoCA is more sensitive to detecting forms of cognitive dysfunction seen in Parkinson disease
questions.solution: Correct Option C - The MoCA is more sensitive to detecting forms of cognitive dysfunction seen in Parkinson disease: The MMSE is the “classic”/"go to" cognitive battery used by many clinicians in the office and hospital setting to screen patients for cognitive dysfunction. It is a very well suited for use in the Alzheimer Disease (AD) population but often falls short in patients with mild cognitive dysfunction and in those with non-AD forms of dementia, including dementia in the PD population. Fortunately, the MoCA does better in these populations. Incorrect Options: Option A - The MMSE yields many “false positive” results when used in well-educated subjects: The statement that "The MMSE yields many 'false positive' results when used in well-educated subjects" is not accurate. The MMSE is generally considered less sensitive to cognitive changes in well-educated individuals, which may lead to false-negative results rather than false positives. Option B - The MoCA requires less training in test administration than does the MMSE: The MoCA includes assessments of executive function, abstraction, and visuospatial abilities that are not well captured on the MMSE. However, both provide a comparable assessment of language, rendering option d inaccurate. The MoCA may yield false positive results in subjects without a college education but there is no evidence to suggest that the MMSE yields false positive results in well-educated subjects. On the contrary well-educated subjects are often able to compensate on cognitive testing and so one might expect more false negative results on cognitive testing in this population, particularly earlier on in their disease course. Training is important for practitioners administering the MoCA, as the test already carries an elevated false positive rate in certain subjects, and improper administration only adds to this limitation. Option D - The MoCA provides a more robust assessment of language dysfunction than does the MMSE: The statement that "The MoCA provides a more robust assessment of language dysfunction than does the MMSE" is not entirely accurate. Both the MoCA and MMSE assess language and other cognitive domains. The MoCA might have slightly more language-related tasks, but it's not necessarily a more robust assessment of language dysfunction. @Neet_pg_bot

Despite this, her DAS 28 score at 3 months was 5.8 and at 4 months her DAS 28 score was 6.1. She is being considered for anti-TNF therapy but on further questioning, it emerges her father suffered from tuberculosis when she was growing up. She did not receive the BCG during adolescence.
Heaf test Grade 0 (minimal response)
Chest X-ray: Clear lung fields, normal cardiac silhouette
Interferon Gamma Release assay: negative
Which of the following treatment options would be most appropriate?

options.label: B
options.text: Isoniazid for 6 months and start adalimumab

questions.answerText: Isoniazid for 6 months and start adalimumab
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Isoniazid for 6 months and start adalimumab: Current guidelines for anti-TNF therapy recommend isoniazid prophylaxis for 6 months for patients born in areas at high risk of tuberculosis, particularly the Indian Subcontinent and SubSaharan Africa if the risk of tuberculosis exceeds the risk of isoniazid toxicity1. An alternative prophylactic regimen suggested is rifampicin and isoniazid for a shorter period of 3 months. Concurrent immunosuppression makes interpretation of the tuberculin skin test unreliable. Incorrect Options: Option A - Adalimumab: While adalimumab might be an appropriate treatment option for this patient's rheumatoid arthritis, her history of potential tuberculosis exposure requires careful consideration. Starting adalimumab without addressing the tuberculosis risk could be unsafe due to the risk of reactivating latent tuberculosis. Option C - Leflunomide: Leflunomide would be an alternative drug, but this lady meets the DAS criteria for anti-TNF. Option D - Prednisolone: Prednisolone is not a long-term treatment due to the side effects @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male comes to the trauma center after a roll-over motor vehicle accident with abdominal pain. FAST exam is positive in the suprapubic view. The patients vitals are BP 125/82 mm of Hg, HR 85/min, RR18/min, Sat 98% on room air. The decision is made to obtain a CT scan of the abdomen, which shows fluid in the pelvis with concern for traumatic bladder rupture. What is the next step in evaluation of this injury to determine need for possible surgical management?

options.label: C
options.text: Repeat CT scan with IV, oral and rectal contrast

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Retrograde urethrogram: This patient has findings on CT scan that are concerning for traumatic bladder rupture. Further evaluation of this injury is needed as management varies based on the severity of the injury. Most intra-peritoneal bladder injuries require surgical intervention, while extra-peritoneal bladder injury can often be managed non-surgically. CT cystogram is the best test to evaluate for bladder injury, however, plain film cystogram is acceptable too. In this test, contrast is injected into the bladder through a foley catheter. Thus, it is very important to first perform a retrograde urethrogram to ensure there is no damage to the urethra prior to passing the foley catheter. Images from CT cystogram evaluate the integrity of the bladder wall and can be used to determine the severity of bladder injury. Incorrect Options: Option A - Abdominal ultrasound: Abdominal ultrasound would be less accurate than a CT cystogram to evaluate bladder injury. In the setting of trauma, ultrasound is most commonly used to perform a FAST exam to quickly evaluate for abdominal trauma from the bedside. Option C - Repeat CT scan with IV, oral and rectal contrast: Repeat CT scan with IV, oral and rectal contrast would give a considerable amount of information concerning intra-abdominal trauma, however, in this case a more focused study is warranted. Option D - CT cystogram: The NEXT best step would be the urethrogram to ensure patency of the urethra prior to passing the foley. The CT cystogram is the best diagnostic test. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man comes to the hospital because of a 2-day history of intermittent bloody urine. He has not had dysuria or abdominal pain. There has been no change in urine output or urinary frequency. He has also had a runny nose, dry cough, and sore throat for the past 4 days. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. His temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F), pulse is 70/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary and abdominal examinations show no abnormalities. There is flank tenderness to palpation bilaterally. Laboratory studies show: Leukocyte count 11,200/mm3 Serum Urea nitrogen 10 mg/dL Creatinine 1.5 mg/dL Complement C3 111 mg/dL (N = 80–160) Urine Blood 3+ Protein 2+ RBC 12/hpf with dysmorphic features RBC casts numerous Ultrasonography of the kidneys shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?

			12/hpf with dysmorphic features
			RBC casts

Ultrasonography of the kidneys shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - IgA nephropathy: This patient is most likely suffering from IgA nephropathy. IgA nephropathy most commonly manifests during the second or third decade of life with recurrent episodes of gross hematuria, flank pain, low-grade fever, and nephritic syndrome, usually during or immediately following (within days) an upper respiratory tract infection. Patients typically have asymptomatic urinary abnormalities, such as microhematuria, between these episodes. The most likely etiology of these findings is an increased number of defective circulating IgA antibodies, the synthesis of which is triggered by mucosal infections (e.g., pharyngitis). These IgA antibodies form immune complexes that deposit in the mesangium of the renal glomerulus, leading to glomerulonephritis (type III hypersensitivity reaction). A renal biopsy provides a definitive diagnosis but is usually only indicated if there are signs of severe or progressive disease (e.g., proteinuria > 0.5–1 g/24 h, hypertension, elevated creatinine levels). Treatment involves monitoring kidney function and initiating treatment if the disease progresses, such as using ACE inhibitors for hypertension and proteinuria and immunosuppressive therapy in severe cases. Incorrect Options: Option A - Goodpasture syndrome: This statement is incorrect as anti-glomerular basement membrane disease (Goodpasture syndrome) most commonly affects young adult male individuals and can manifest with nephritic-range proteinuria and hematuria . However, Goodpasture syndrome also affects the pulmonary capillary basement membrane (in most cases, due to autoantibodies against collagen type IV), leading to hemoptysis, cough, and dyspnea, none of which is seen here. Option B - Minimal change of disease: This statement is incorrect, as minimal change disease (MCD) often occurs following a viral infection. However, MCD manifests with nephrotic-range proteinuria and oedema, which is not seen here. Finally, MCD most commonly affects children < 6 years of age. Option D - Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis: This statement is incorrect as post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) can manifest with hypertension and gross hematuria following upper respiratory tract infection. PSGN is more common in children and usually manifests 10–30 days after an acute infection. Furthermore, C3 complement levels are low in PSGN, whereas this patient's C3 complement levels are normal. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 53-year-old male patient with a long history of alcohol abuse is undergoing evaluation for chronic watery diarrhea for 4 months and recent unintended weight loss of 20 kg over 6 months. He complains of fatigue and anorexia. Exam reveals loss of subcutaneous fat and muscular atrophy in the upper arms and legs. Oropharyngeal exam is significant for glossitis, and he has moderate ascites with bilateral 2+ pedal edema. Handgrip strength is diminished. Neurological exam reveals decreased proprioceptive and vibratory sensation in both feet. Laboratory studies are significant for hemoglobin 9.0 g/L with MCV 105. Serum albumin is 2.1 g/dL, and prealbumin is 0.02 g/L (0.2-0.4). Which of the following is most likely to be the primary factor underlying the patient’s malnutrition?

Neurological exam reveals decreased proprioceptive and vibratory sensation in both feet. Laboratory studies are significant for hemoglobin 9.0 g/L with MCV 105. Serum albumin is 2.1 g/dL, and prealbumin is 0.02 g/L (0.2-0.4). Which of the following is most likely to be the primary factor underlying the patient’s malnutrition?

options.label: B
options.text: Pancreatic insufficiency due to alcohol abuse

options.label: C
options.text: Increasing liver dysfunction with reduced albumin synthesis

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Poor intake with malabsorption: Individuals who consume a large amount of alcohol over a sustained period of time may consume up to 50% of their caloric intake as alcohol. Alcohol also increases serum leptin, which may further reduce dietary intake. Chronic alcohol ingestion reduces absorption of nutrients, and damage to the intestinal mucosa contributes to bacterial overgrowth and altered intestinal motility. Protein-calorie malnutrition is usually seen in patients with advanced alcoholic liver disease and is associated with a poor prognosis. In this patient, macrocytic anemia suggests cobalamin or thiamine deficiency. B12 (cobalamin) and folate deficiency are both causes of megaloblastic anemia, but only cobalamin causes neurological changes. However, cobalamin deficiency is unusual in the absence of chronic pancreatitis. Thiamine deficiency may be found in up to 80% of patients who chronically use alcohol and is also associated with peripheral neuropathy. Glossitis suggests folate deficiency. In patients with malnutrition and chronic alcohol use disorder, thiamine, folic acid, and vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) should be administered. Incorrect Options: Option A - Protein-losing gastroenteropathy : Protein-losing gastroenteropathy may occur as the result of mucosal damage or due to increased lymphatic pressure in the stomach or small bowel. This diagnosis should be part of the differential in patients with low albumin without another cause. Although it may be a contributing factor in some patients with chronic alcohol abuse, it is less likely to be the cause of this patient’s malnutrition. Option B - Pancreatic insufficiency due to alcohol abuse : Although pancreatic insufficiency may contribute to malnutrition in patients with chronic alcohol use disorder, it is less likely to be the major contributing factor. Option C - Increasing liver dysfunction with reduced albumin synthesis : Although liver dysfunction contributes to reduced protein synthesis, it is not the primary etiology of the patient’s malnutrition. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease, hypertension, and smoking is brought to the emergency department with severe midline abdominal pain. The pain started acutely 30 minutes ago and is not associated with nausea or vomiting. Vital signs are notable for a heart rate of 120 beats per minute and a blood pressure of 85/55 mm Hg. On physical examination, the patient has a pulsatile abdominal mass and poor peripheral perfusion. Which of the following describes this patient’s underlying pathology leading to this acute event?
questions.stemHtml:
A 68-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease, hypertension, and smoking is brought to the emergency department with severe midline abdominal pain. The pain started acutely 30 minutes ago and is not associated with nausea or vomiting. Vital signs are notable for a heart rate of 120 beats per minute and a blood pressure of 85/55 mm Hg. On physical examination, the patient has a pulsatile abdominal mass and poor peripheral perfusion.
Which of the following describes this patient’s underlying pathology leading to this acute event?

options.label: B
options.text: Separation of the intima from the arterial wall

options.label: D
options.text: Cellular infiltration and inflammation of the aorta

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Segmental full-thickness arterial dilation: Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is a progressive dilation of the abdominal aorta that appears generally in Caucasian men over the age of 65. Hypertension and smoking are important risk factors for the development of AAA. These patients are often asymptomatic and are followed with periodic abdominal ultrasounds to determine if surgical intervention is necessary. If the patient is symptomatic, non-ruptured AAA may be associated with mild abdominal pain or compression of surrounding structures. AAA rupture is the most feared complication and leads to severe abdominal pain, hypotension, and a pulsatile abdominal mass . Active smoking, aneurysms >5.5 cm in size, and rapid expansion increase the risk of rupture . AAA rupture requires urgent intervention. Patients who are hemodynamically unstable need emergent surgery. Incorrect Options: Option B - Separation of the intima from the arterial wall: Separation of the intima from the arterial wall describes aortic dissection. While acute dissection may resemble aneurysm rupture, hypotension and a pulsatile mass make AAA more likely. Option C - Full-thickness gastric ulceration and perforation: Full-thickness gastric ulceration and perforation describe a perforated gastric ulcer. This condition may be confused for AAA rupture in a more hemodynamically stable patient. This patient’s multiple AAA risk factors and pulsatile abdominal mass make AAA more likely. Option D - Cellular infiltration and inflammation of the aorta: Cellular infiltration and inflammation of the aorta describe aortitis, which may occur in vasculitis such as Takayasu arteritis or infectious conditions such as Bartonella. This patient’s multiple AAA risk factors and pulsatile abdominal mass make AAA more likely. @Neet_pg_bot

He has been taking immunosuppressive medications to prevent organ rejection. However, a lymph node biopsy confirms the diagnosis of post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD), a condition that can occur due to abnormal growth of lymphocytes in individuals who have undergone solid organ transplantation. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

questions.solution: Correct Option B- Initiate chemotherapy: PTLD is a potential complication of solid organ transplantation associated with the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). The clinical presentation can vary widely, ranging from asymptomatic disease to aggressive lymphoma. Treatment options for PTLD depend on the disease's severity, the lymphoma's location, and the patient's overall health status. Incorrect Options: Option A - Discontinuing immunosuppressive therapy: It is an essential first step in managing PTLD, as it can help reduce the risk of further lymphoma growth. However, this alone is insufficient in most cases , and additional therapies such as chemotherapy or radiation therapy may be necessary. Option C- Surgical resection of the affected lymph nodes: It may be considered in some localized PTLD, particularly if the lymphoma is confined to a single area and can be safely removed. However, this is not a first-line management strategy and is typically reserved for cases where other treatments have failed. Option D- Radiation therapy: It may be helpful in some cases of PTLD, particularly if the lymphoma is localized and can be targeted with radiation. However, this is not a first-line management strategy and is typically reserved for cases where other treatments have failed. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A middle-aged woman complains of chest pain and a squeezing sensation in her chest that spreads to her left shoulder. The pain started 15 minutes ago when she was watching television. She has experienced similar pain before, but the pain usually went away after a couple of minutes. Her vital signs indicate an elevated heart rate, blood pressure within the normal range, and slightly increased respiratory rate. An ECG reveals ST-segment elevations in the inferior leads. Two successive blood draws for serum troponins are negative, and an ECG 30 minutes later shows no abnormalities. What is the most appropriate long-term treatment for this patient's symptoms?

Two successive blood draws for serum troponins are negative, and an ECG 30 minutes later shows no abnormalities. What is the most appropriate long-term treatment for this patient's symptoms?
questions.solution: Correct Option B- Diltiazem: This patient’s clinical scenario indicates the diagnosis of vasospastic or Prinzmetal angina. The best strategy for the long-term management of this disorder is using calcium channel clockers i.e., diltiazem. This type of angina is treated by calcium channel blocker which is preventive for this disorder. Nitrates can be used as abortive therapy but it is not used for long-term management of this disorder. Smoking and the use of stimulant substances like cocaine and amphetamines can lead to this disorder. A hallmark feature of this type of angina is the transient disruption of blood supply to the heart. The patient will show an ST-segment elevation or depression during the episode but there will not be any elevation in troponins. Also, the ST segment changes will revert to normal soon after the episode ends. That is why Holter monitoring of the ECG can help in making a diagnosis. Lastly, coronary angiography will not show any stenosis of the vessels thus ruling out coronary artery disease. The first choice of therapy for this disorder is calcium channel blockers which are used long-term. Long-acting nitrates can also be used; however, sublingual nitrates are only used as abortive therapy during the episode. Incorrect Options: Option A- Sublingual Nitrates: These are also used for symptomatic relief in acute coronary artery disease and vasospastic angina. But their long-term use in vasospastic angina is not beneficial. Option C- Clopidogrel P2Y12 receptor blockers are used for the purpose of preventing stent thrombosis after stents are placed following an episode of myocardial infarction. They do not have utility in vasospastic angina. Option D- Metoprolol: Beta blockers are contraindicated for use in vasospastic angina. There is a theoretical concern that they can block the beta-mediated vasodilation receptors of beta-2 that can cause unopposed vasospasm during anginal episodes and make the situation worse. @Neet_pg_bot

Option D- Reducing dialysis treatment frequency: It may also not be appropriate in end-of-life care as the focus is on providing comfort rather than treatment. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Regular narrow QRS complexes: Following are the EKG findings seen in supraventricular tachycardia. Regular narrow QRS complexes: The QRS complex width is typically < 120 ms because the electrical impulses originate in or above the atria and travel through the normal conduction system of the heart. Absent or abnormal P waves: P waves may be difficult to distinguish or absent due to the rapid rate of atrial depolarization. P-wave hidden within the QRS complex: When the electrical activity of the atria and ventricles overlap, the P wave may be hidden within the QRS complex. Inverted P waves: In some cases, the P waves may be inverted, which is seen in junctional tachycardia or AV nodal reentrant tachycardia. Shortened PR interval: The PR interval may be shortened due to the rapid conduction through the AV node. Normal or increased QT interval: The QT interval, which reflects the duration of ventricular repolarization, is typically normal or slightly prolonged in SVT. No ST-segment or T-wave abnormalities: ST-segment or T-wave changes are not typically seen in SVT. Incorrect Options: Option A - Tall T-waves: The T wave on an electrocardiogram becomes tall when there is increased electrical activity in the ventricles of the heart. It is mainly caused by hyperkalemia, ventricular hypertrophy, myocardial ischemia, and drug side effects such as digoxin. Option B - ST-elevation: ST segment is the period between the end of the QRS complex and the beginning of the T wave. It is usually elevated from normal in cases of acute myocardial infarction, pericarditis, and pulmonary embolism. Option C - Delta Waves: Delta waves appear as slurring or widening of the QRS complex on an ECG. Specifically, delta waves are seen in patients with Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome , a condition in which there is an additional electrical pathway in the heart. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C- Sodium hypochlorite: Sodium hypochlorite is a commonly used household cleaning agent that is highly toxic when ingested. It can cause severe damage to the gastrointestinal system, respiratory system, and kidneys. Ingestion of sodium hypochlorite can result in symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and difficulty breathing. The severity of the symptoms is related to the amount of toxin ingested and the duration of exposure. In this clinical scenario, the patient presents with symptoms of acute kidney injury, including elevated serum creatinine and BUN levels, anion gap metabolic acidosis, and hematuria and proteinuria on urinalysis. The patient also has a history of ingesting a household cleaning agent, suggesting that the renal injury is due to exposure to a toxin. The clinical findings are consistent with the toxic effects of sodium hypochlorite. The anion gap metabolic acidosis seen in the patient is likely due to chloride ions in the toxin, which are converted to hydrochloric acid in the body . The hematuria and proteinuria on urinalysis indicate renal injury, which can occur due to exposure to certain toxins, including sodium hypochlorite. The management of sodium hypochlorite toxicity includes supportive care and decontamination. The patient should receive intravenous fluids to maintain adequate hydration and support kidney function . Activated charcoal may help bind the toxin and prevent further absorption. Hemodialysis may be required in severe cases to remove the toxin from the bloodstream and improve renal function . He was diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis 2 months back and was started on anti-tuberculosis therapy. On examination, there is conjunctival pallor and dry lips with cracks at the angle of the mouth. Sensory examination shows decreased sensation of light touch and pinpricked in the lower limb, and motor examination is unremarkable. questions.solution: Correct Option D - Pyridoxine : A deficiency of pyridoxine is associated with the development of paresthesias and sideroblastic/microcytic anaemia ( microcytic anaemia can cause cheilosis and glossitis) Patients taking anti-tubercular therapy (ATT) can develop pyridoxine deficiency due to isoniazid toxicity Pyridoxine is a co-factor that is required for the synthesis of neurotransmitters and the heme group of haemoglobin Hence deficiency of pyridoxine results in peripheral neuropathy, mainly affecting the sensations and anaemia Generally, pyridoxine deficiency is rare; however, in those patients who are taking ATT, isoniazid competes with pyridoxine in neurotransmitter synthesis To prevent pyridoxine deficiency due to isoniazid, supplemental pyridoxine is added as an adjuvant therapy In addition to that, INH is also associated with hepatotoxicity that presents with nausea, vomiting, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain Other relatively less common side effects of INH therapy are psychosis, optic neuritis, pellagra, metabolic acidosis, etc Incorrect Options: Option A - Folic acid : Folic acid deficiency gives rise to megaloblastic anaemia rather than microcytic or sideroblastic anaemia. Folic acid deficiency does not result in peripheral sensory neuropathy Option B - Vitamin B12: Vitamin B12 deficiency can lead to the development of peripheral neuropathy. However, in addition to peripheral neuropathy, other neurological manifestations are also present, i.e. ataxia, cognitive impairment, irritability, etc Vitamin B12 deficiency gives rise to macrocytic anaemia rather than microcytic anaemia Option C - Iron : Deficiency of iron results in microcytic anaemia However, iron deficiency is not associated with the development of neurological manifestations @Neet_pg_bot

Correct Option D - Pyridoxine :

  • A deficiency of pyridoxine is associated with the development of paresthesias and sideroblastic/microcytic anaemia ( microcytic anaemia can cause cheilosis and glossitis)
  • Patients taking anti-tubercular therapy (ATT) can develop pyridoxine deficiency due to isoniazid toxicity 
  • Pyridoxine is a co-factor that is required for the synthesis of neurotransmitters and the heme group of haemoglobin 
  • Hence deficiency of pyridoxine results in peripheral neuropathy, mainly affecting the sensations and anaemia 
  • Generally, pyridoxine deficiency is rare; however, in those patients who are taking ATT, isoniazid competes with pyridoxine in neurotransmitter synthesis
  • To prevent pyridoxine deficiency due to isoniazid, supplemental pyridoxine is added as an adjuvant therapy 
  • In addition to that, INH is also associated with hepatotoxicity that presents with nausea, vomiting, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain
  • Other relatively less common side effects of INH therapy are psychosis, optic neuritis, pellagra, metabolic acidosis, etc

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Folic acid :

  • Folic acid deficiency gives rise to megaloblastic anaemia rather than microcytic or sideroblastic anaemia.
  • Folic acid deficiency does not result in peripheral sensory neuropathy 

Option B - Vitamin B12:

  • Vitamin B12 deficiency can lead to the development of peripheral neuropathy. However, in addition to peripheral neuropathy, other neurological manifestations are also present, i.e. ataxia, cognitive impairment, irritability, etc 
  • Vitamin B12 deficiency gives rise to macrocytic anaemia rather than microcytic anaemia

Option C - Iron :

  • Deficiency of iron results in microcytic anaemia 
  • However, iron deficiency is not associated with the development of neurological manifestations

The laboratory results revealed anemia. Which of the following is the cause of this patient's current condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- Decreased erythropoietin: Chronic kidney disease results from the gradual decline in the function of the kidney function. Besides maintaining the electrolyte balance and excretion of metabolic wastes, the kidneys are also involved in the metabolism and management of hormones. Erythropoietin is one of the hormones that plays an essential role in the proliferation and differentiation of red blood cells. In chronic kidney disease, there is a failure of the production of erythropoietin which results in anemia. The anemia can result in the symptoms of shortness of breath, fatigue, and tiredness. On physical examination, the patient will look pale. Incorrect Options: Option A- Hemolysis: Hemolysis can destroy the red blood cells causing anemia which can produce the symptoms of shortness of breath and fatigue. Some of the causes of hemolysis are infections, genetic disease, DIC, etc. However, in chronic kidney disease patients, the anemia is caused by the absence of erythropoietin. Option B- Iron deficiency: Iron deficiency is one of the common causes of anemia which can result in microcytic anemia. Some of the causes of iron deficiency anemia are malabsorption, dietary deficiency, infections, heavy menstrual bleeding, tumors, etc. Option C- Bone marrow fibrosis: Bone marrow fibrosis can also cause anemia because bone marrow is the main site for the production of red blood cells. In this condition, the bone marrow is replaced by connective tissue. Tear-shaped red blood cells can result from bone marrow fibrosis. This patient's anemia is not due to bone marrow fibrosis, instead, it is caused by the absence of erythropoietin. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Liver toxicity

  • Tetracyclines bind with the 30S subunit of ribosomes and inhibit bacterial protein synthesis. They are not recommended to be used for prophylaxis in children with VUR.

questions.solution: Correct Option D – Dexamethasone: This patient most likely has laryngotracheobronchitis or croup . Croup affects approximately 3% of children six months to three years of age and is responsible for 7% of hospitalizations annually for acute respiratory illness and fever in children less than five years of age. Croup results from upper respiratory obstruction caused by swelling of the larynx, trachea, and bronchi. Clinically, it is characterized by a barking cough and inspiratory stridor. Tachycardia is common. Respiratory rate may be increased above the normal rate for patients in the age group of 6 months to three years, typically 20 to 30 breaths per minute. More severe cases may result in retractions, nasal flaring, and cyanosis. Parainfluenza type 1 is the most common cause of croup , but other causes include influenza, respiratory syncytial virus, rhinovirus, and adenovirus. Fever, respiratory distress, with worsening of the barking cough at night are all common. Depending upon severity, treatment includes humidified oxygen, l-isomer or racemic epinephrine nebulizer, and steroid therapy with oral or intramuscular dexamethasone. Dexamethasone is usually adequate in mild cases. Admission is required in some cases due to either respiratory distress or hypoxia. Epiglottitis, although decreasing in incidence since the introduction of the Haemophilus influenza vaccine, should be ruled out. Incorrect Options: Option A - Amoxicillin: Amoxicillin is not indicated in this viral process. Option B and C: Ipratropium and albuterol are both used for cases of lower respiratory obstructive diseases such as asthma or bronchitis, but these are not necessary in the absence of wheezes on pulmonary examination. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 39-year-old female with a history of intravenous heroin use presents with generalised body swelling and fatigue for 1 month. Urinalysis shows proteinuria in the range of nephrotic syndrome. Renal biopsy shows the following findings on light microscopy: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option A- Focal segmental glomerular sclerosis (FSGS): The patient presents with the clinical features and investigative findings of FSGS. FSGS affects juxtamedullary nephrons initially. As segmental involvement is characteristic , an inadequate sample can miss focal lesions. On histopathology, FSGS presents with sclerosis, hyalinosis, and synechiae formation (as shown above). This results in segmental occlusion of glomerular capillaries . Effacement of foot processes is a significant finding in electron microscopy. No abnormalities of the basement membrane are seen. IgM and C3 stains are seen in the sclerotic areas on immunofluorescence. FSGS can be divided into five types based on histology : Perihilar : The sclerotic lesion is seen at the vascular region of the glomerulus. Mild effacement of foot processes occurs. Tip: The segmental lesion involves the tubular pole of the glomerulus. Diffuse effacement of foot processes occurs. Cellular: The glomerulus is hypercellular ( epithelial and endocapillary hyperplasia) . Diffuse effacement of foot processes occurs. Collapsing: Hypertrophy and hyperplasia of visceral epithelial cells cause a collapse of the glomerular tuft. Diffuse effacement of foot processes occurs. Not otherwise specified: Has no specific morphology and does not fit into any other category. A variable degree of foot process effacement occurs. questions.solution: Correct Option C - ADP antagonist at the P2Y12 receptor: Clopidogrel, and ticlopidine, act as ADP antagonists at the P2Y12 receptor on platelets. When activated this receptor activates the glycoprotein IIb/IIIa complex, which serves as the major receptor for fibrinogen on the platelet membrane, and therefore inhibition of this cascade inhibits platelet aggregation. Clopidogrel also irreversibly modifies the P2Y12 receptor so that it is no longer active and therefore the duration of the drug effect is for the lifespan of the platelet (7-10 days). Incorrect Options: Option A - Cyclooxygenase inhibition: Cyclooxygenase (COX) inhibitors are commonly referred to as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). They work by blocking the production of prostaglandins, which are involved in inflammation and pain. Clopidogrel does not inhibit cyclooxygenase; its mechanism of action is different. Option B - Direct thrombin inhibition: Direct thrombin inhibitors, like dabigatran, directly target and inhibit the enzyme thrombin, which is crucial in the blood coagulation cascade. Clopidogrel does not directly inhibit thrombin. Option D - Enhanced antithrombin III activity: Antithrombin III is a natural anticoagulant that inhibits several clotting factors in the blood. Some anticoagulant drugs work by enhancing the activity of antithrombin III. Clopidogrel does not affect antithrombin III. Option E - Vitamin K epoxide reductase inhibition: Vitamin K epoxide reductase is an enzyme involved in the recycling of vitamin K, which is necessary for the synthesis of certain clotting factors. questions.stem: A 57-year-old man presents in the cardiac emergency room with chest discomfort, fever and malaise for the last 3 days. He describes his pain as sharp, non-radiating and pleuritic pain that worsens with lying flat and improves with bending forward. He is currently recovering from an acute myocardial infarction 3 weeks back. On examination, his vital signs are normal, and auscultation of the precordium reveals a pericardial friction rub. His ECG shows diffuse ST elevation with concavity upwards. His WBC count, ESR and CRP is raised. Considering the likely possibility, which of the following drug should be given?
questions.stemHtml: A 57-year-old man presents in the cardiac emergency room with chest discomfort, fever and malaise for the last 3 days. He describes his pain as sharp, non-radiating and pleuritic pain that worsens with lying flat and improves with bending forward. He is currently recovering from an acute myocardial infarction 3 weeks back. On examination, his vital signs are normal, and auscultation of the precordium reveals a pericardial friction rub. His ECG shows diffuse ST elevation with concavity upwards. His WBC count, ESR and CRP is raised. Considering the likely possibility, which of the following drug should be given?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Aspirin: The clinical scenario points to the diagnosis of Dressler’s syndrome due to the presence of typical symptoms 3 weeks following myocardial infarction. Dressler’s syndrome or postmyocardial infarction syndrome is a specific type of pericarditis due to injury to the pericardium or myocytes, as in myocardial infarction. The underlying pathophysiology of Dressler syndrome is unknown, but the proposed mechanism is the primary injury to mesothelial cells of the pericardium and the presence of blood in the pericardial sac. This triggers an immune-mediated response resulting in the deposition of immune complexes in the pericardium, lungs and pleura. A definitive diagnosis is made with raised ESR, CRP, WBC count and anti-cardiomyocyte antibodies. The treatment of choice is aspirin which decreases inflammation. The recommended dose of aspirin in Dressler’s syndrome is 650 mg 4 hourly. Patients with Dressler's syndrome complicated with pericardial effusion should be initially managed with therapeutic pericardiocentesis to prevent impending tamponade. Incorrect Options: Option A - Ibuprofen: Ibuprofen and other NSAIDs should be avoided in patients with Dressler's syndrome. These drugs increase the incidence of impaired healing of infarct, ventricular rupture, and increased coronary vascular resistance in the post-MI period. Option C - Prednisolone: Prednisolone and any other steroid should be avoided in patients with Dressler’s syndrome. These drugs increase the incidence of impaired healing of infarct, ventricular rupture, and increased coronary vascular resistance in the post-MI period. Option D - Heparin: Heparin should be avoided in patients with Dressler’s syndrome. Heparin administration can cause bleeding into the pericardial sac, increasing the risk of cardiac tamponade. @Neet_pg_bot

Typical anthracycline containing regimens used in other aggressive lymphomas have proven inferior in treating ENK/T lymphomas, potentially explained by high levels of P-glycoprotein expression (Yamaguchi M, et al. questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old male with a history of hypertension and chronic kidney disease (CKD) presents to the emergency department with confusion and altered mental status. He has missed his last few hemodialysis sessions and reports feeling unwell for the past few days. On examination, he appears disoriented and unable to follow commands. The patient's neurological examination reveals asterixis and myoclonus. Laboratory tests reveal a serum creatinine level of 6.5 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen level of 80 mg/dL, and serum potassium level of 6.8 mEq/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option B- Uremic encephalopathy: In this scenario, the patient's high serum creatinine, BUN, and potassium levels indicate chronic kidney disease (CKD) , and the presence of asterixis and myoclonus suggests uremic encephalopathy. Uremic encephalopathy is a neurological disorder in patients with end-stage kidney disease. It is caused by the accumulation of toxic metabolic waste products normally excreted by the kidneys. The exact mechanism by which uremic encephalopathy develops is not fully understood. Still, it involves a combination of factors, including the accumulation of uremic toxins in the brain, electrolyte imbalances, and changes in cerebral blood flow. Some common symptoms of uremic encephalopathy include: Confusion Disorientation Irritability Fatigue Difficulty concentrating Seizures Coma The diagnosis of uremic encephalopathy is based on clinical presentation and laboratory tests, such as blood tests to measure urea levels , creatinine, and electrolytes. Imaging studies, such as a CT scan or MRI, may be performed to rule out other causes of neurological symptoms . T reat ing uremic encephalopathy involves addressing the underlying cause of the condition, typically advanced kidney disease. This may involve dialysis or a kidney transplant to remove the accumulated toxins from the bloodstream. In addition, medications may be used to manage symptoms, such as antiepileptic drugs for seizures or sedatives for agitation. Prevention of uremic encephalopathy in patients with CKD involves proper management of the underlying kidney disease, including monitoring and controlling blood pressure, maintaining fluid and electrolyte balance, and avoiding nephrotoxic medications. Incorrect Options: Option A- Cerebral infarction: Cerebral infarction is caused by the blockage of blood vessels in the brain, resulting in decreased blood flow and oxygen supply to the affected area. It typically presents with focal deficits such as weakness, numbness, or difficulty speaking rather than the diffuse neurological symptoms seen in uremic encephalopathy. questions.stemHtml: A 42-year-old gentleman k/c/o DCLD, post liver transplantation from an ABO unmatched unrelated donor with hb on POD 5 is noted to be 6.2 g/dL, from a baseline of 9g/dl.
