The donor is CMV negative as is the recipient. A review of his peripheral smear does not reveal schistocytes. There is no evidence of blood loss. He is started on cyclosporine and prednisone. What is the likely cause of the patient’s anemia?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Passenger lymphocyte syndrome : Passenger Lymphocyte Syndrome (PLS) is a phenomenon that occurs after solid organ transplantation, particularly when the donor and recipient are ABO-incompatible. PLS involves the temporary presence of donor lymphocytes in the recipient's bloodstream, which can trigger an immune response against the recipient's own blood cells. In the context of solid organ transplantation: Donor lymphocytes, including T-cells, can be present in the graft. After transplantation, these donor lymphocytes enter the recipient's bloodstream. The donor lymphocytes recognize the recipient's blood cells as foreign due to ABO incompatibility. This recognition triggers an immune response against the recipient's blood cells, leading to hemolysis and anemia. The clinical presentation of PLS may include anemia, jaundice, elevated LDH, decreased haptoglobin, and sometimes elevated bilirubin. Peripheral smear may not show schistocytes, distinguishing it from other forms of hemolytic anemia. Incorrect Options: Option A - Drug-Induced Hemolysis: While some medications can cause immune-mediated hemolysis, the patient's presentation, along with the history of liver transplantation and ABO incompatibility, points towards PLS. Option C - Drug-Induced Microangiopathic Hemolytic Anemia (MAHA): This choice implies the involvement of small blood vessels, but the patient's presentation doesn't strongly suggest microangiopathy. Additionally, the absence of schistocytes on peripheral smear also makes this choice less likely. Option D - Drug-Induced MAHA: Similar to the previous choice, this option doesn't align well with the patient's clinical presentation, which is more consistent with PLS associated with ABO incompatibility. @Neet_pg_bot

			Blood

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Salt retention In this case, a woman presents to the physician with dark urine, heaviness in both legs, decreased concentration, and fatigue. The patient has a history of malaria and on examination, there is pretibial oedema bilaterally . The scenario indicates that the patient has membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis due to malarial infection . MPGN can present with the features of both nephrotic and nephritic syndrome . There are further divided into 3 types. Type 1 involves the deposition of immune complexes and complements in the kidney. Type 2 involves the deposition of C3 byproducts into the basement membrane and type 3 also has deposits of immune complexes as well as a complement in the subendothelial, and subepithelial space. The patient in this case features nephritic syndrome due to MPGN which results in damage to the glomerular capillary walls. The disturbance of the glomerular filtration barrier can lead to a decrease in the filtration rate causing salt retention . Proteins also pass to the urine which can cause inflammation. Incorrect Options: Option A - Increased peripheral capillary permeability Increased peripheral capillary permeability is most of the time caused by allergic reactions, inflammation, or tissue damage . The tissue damage can mostly occur due to burn injuries . The resulting oedema is not bilateral and is usually localised. Bilateral oedema of the legs can occur in patients who have a systemic capillary leak. Option B - Lymphatic obstruction Lymphoedema is the building up of lymph in the body tissues due to obstruction in the lymphatic system. It mostly affects the arms and legs but can also be present in the abdomen, neck and genitals. It presents as swelling to the affected area with recurring infections and hardening of the skin. They are mostly caused due to cancer, parasites, surgery, and radiation therapy. Treatment depends on oedema and fibrosis with the help of compression bandages or surgery in severe cases . Option C - Paraneoplastic erythropoietin production Paraneoplastic production of erythropoietin can occur in patients who suffer from hepatocellular carcinoma and renal cell carcinoma . Increased levels of EPO can cause a hypercoagulable state that can result in thrombosis . Renal cell carcinoma can also present with flank pain and hematuria . People with hepatitis infection are at greater risk of developing hepatocellular carcinoma. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 42-year-old patient presents with recurring episodes of unexplained fever, fatigue, and mild hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory tests reveal decreased levels of CD16 and CD56 markers. Which of the following conditions is most likely to be associated with the findings in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 42-year-old patient presents with recurring episodes of unexplained fever, fatigue, and mild hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory tests reveal decreased levels of CD16 and CD56 markers. Which of the following conditions is most likely to be associated with the findings in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Natural killer (NK) cell deficiency: Natural killer cells are a type of immune cell that plays a critical role in the immune system's defense against viral infections and tumor cells. Deficiencies in NK cells can lead to recurrent infections, unexplained fever, and reduced ability to control certain pathogens. Decreased levels of CD16 and CD56 markers, which are characteristic markers of NK cells, indicate a deficiency in these cells. Hepatosplenomegaly (enlargement of the liver and spleen) can also occur as a consequence of chronic infections. Thus, the symptoms described in the patient are most consistent with a deficiency in NK cells. Incorrect Options: Option A - Multiple sclerosis: Multiple sclerosis is a neurological disorder characterized by demyelination of nerve cells. It typically presents with symptoms related to the central nervous system, such as motor or sensory deficits, visual disturbances, and coordination problems. It is not associated with the symptoms described in the patient. Option B - Rheumatoid arthritis: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease that primarily affects the joints, leading to joint inflammation, pain, and deformities. While it can cause systemic symptoms like fatigue, it is not typically associated with unexplained fever, hepatosplenomegaly, or decreased levels of CD16 and CD56 markers. Option C - Hemolytic anemia: Hemolytic anemia is a condition where the body destroys red blood cells at an accelerated rate. It can lead to symptoms such as fatigue, pale skin, and jaundice. However, it does not usually cause unexplained fever, hepatosplenomegaly, or alterations in CD16 and CD56 markers. @Neet_pg_bot

The patient is immediately roomed and gowned and vitals are taken. HR is 52bpm. Respirations are shallow and 55 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturation is 88%. options.label: B
options.text: Provide bag valve mask ventilation at 6-8 breaths per minute

options.label: D
options.text: Provide supplemental oxygenation/ventilation and begin chest compressions if HR remains below 60

questions.answerText: Provide supplemental oxygenation/ventilation and begin chest compressions if HR remains below 60
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Provide supplemental oxygenation/ventilation and begin chest compressions if HR remains below 60: Pediatric patients' cardiac outputs are strongly dependent on their heart rate and are generally how their cardiac outputs are augmented. Stroke volume alteration is limited in pediatric patients. So if unable to mount an appropriate response by increasing heart rate, the patient will manifest a more profound state of shock and hypoperfusion than an adult. If adequate oxygenation and ventilation are provided and the HR does not recover to greater than 60, compressions should be started. Incorrect Options: Option A - Chest compressions of 150 per minute: Chest compressions should be administered at a rate of 120 per minute with 30 breaths and 90 compressions per minute giving a ratio of 3:1 or 120 events per minute. Option B - Provide bag valve mask ventilation at 6-8 breaths per minute: Neonatal patients should be ventilated at a 3:1 compressions-to-breaths ratio. If etiology of arrest is likely not respiratory, provider may switch to at 15:2 ratio. Option C - Prepare atropine administration: Atropine is not recommended as a first-line agent in neonatal bradycardia. Generally, epinephrine is the first-line agent recommended @Neet_pg_bot

  • If adequate oxygenation and ventilation are provided and the HR does not recover to greater than 60, compressions should be started.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Chest compressions of 150 per minute: Chest compressions should be administered at a rate of 120 per minute with 30 breaths and 90 compressions per minute giving a ratio of 3:1 or 120 events per minute.

Option B - Provide bag valve mask ventilation at 6-8 breaths per minute: Neonatal patients should be ventilated at a 3:1 compressions-to-breaths ratio. If etiology of arrest is likely not respiratory, provider may switch to at 15:2 ratio.

questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old sailor is transported to a military treatment facility 20 minutes after being engaged in a navy ship collision. He feels the need to defecate but is unable to do so. He appears to be sick. The pulse rate is 140 beats per minute; respirations are 28 beats per minute, and blood pressure is 104/70 mm Hg. Ecchymosis over the scrotum and perineum is found during a pelvic examination. There is tenderness over the suprapubic area and blood at the urethral meatus. A high-riding prostate is revealed by digital rectal examination. An abdominal ultrasound reveals a mildly distended bladder. X-rays of the sacrum reveal fractures in all four pubic rami. questions.solution: Correct Option A: Tearing of posterior urethra Inability to urinate despite desire, suprapubic pain, blood at the urethral meatus, scrotal and perineal ecchymoses, and a high-riding prostate are all symptoms of torn posterior urethra, all of which are present in this patient. This can lead to a condition called pyelonephritis, which can cause scarring of the kidneys and reduce their ability to function properly. Pregnancy complications: UTIs during pregnancy can increase the risk of preterm labour and low birth weight. Urinary tract obstruction: UTIs can cause swelling and inflammation in the urinary tract, which can lead to blockages that prevent urine from flowing properly. This can cause further infections and kidney damage. Antibiotic resistance: Overuse or misuse of antibiotics can lead to the development of antibiotic-resistant strains of bacteria, which can make UTIs more difficult to treat in the future. questions.stemHtml: A 62-year-old gentleman with relapse DLBCL, after BEAM conditioning underwent autologous stem transplant, and presented 10 days later with respiratory distress requiring BiPAP, but afebrile during last 72 hours. CT can shows a diffuse interstitial pattern. Viral serologies and blood cultures are all negative. Weight has been stable since admission. Infectious causes are ruled out with Bronchoscopy. What is the likely etiology?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Engraftment syndrome: Engraftment syndrome, also known as infusion reaction or engraftment reaction, is a common complication following autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT) or allogeneic stem cell transplantation (allo-SCT). It typically occurs within a few days to a few weeks after transplantation and is characterized by a range of symptoms. In this case, the patient's presentation with respiratory distress, diffuse interstitial pattern on CT scan, and negative viral serologies and blood cultures is consistent with engraftment syndrome. Engraftment syndrome can present with respiratory symptoms, fever, and interstitial infiltrates, and it occurs after stem cell transplantation. Engraftment syndrome can manifest with various clinical features, including fever, skin rash, pulmonary symptoms (such as dyspnea), and weight gain. The pulmonary symptoms are often characterized by interstitial infiltrates on imaging, similar to what was seen in the CT scan of this patient. Engraftment syndrome is thought to result from an inflammatory response as the newly infused donor cells begin to engraft and interact with the recipient's tissues Incorrect Options: Option A - HSV pneumonia: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) pneumonia can occur in immunocompromised patients but typically presents with fever and respiratory symptoms along with characteristic imaging findings, such as ground-glass opacities. This patient was afebrile for the last 72 hours, which is not consistent with an active HSV infection. Option B - CMV pneumonitis: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) pneumonitis is another infection that can occur after transplantation. However, it typically presents with fever, respiratory symptoms, and positive CMV serologies, which were negative in this case. Option C - CHF (Congestive Heart Failure): While CHF can present with respiratory distress and may show pulmonary congestion on imaging, the absence of weight gain in this patient and the negative infectious workup make it less likely. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: > Explanation: Mitochondrial myopathies are a group of disorders characterized by impaired oxidative phosphorylation. These disorders result from mutations in mitochondrial DNA or nuclear DNA affecting proteins involved in the electron transport chain. The patient's symptoms, including fatigue, exercise intolerance, and ptosis, are indicative of mitochondrial myopathy rather than Myasthenia gravis. questions.stem: A 63-year-old male with a history of hypertension and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation presents to the emergency department with palpitations and shortness of breath. His vital signs are within normal limits, and EKG reveals atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 63-year-old male with a history of hypertension and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation presents to the emergency department with palpitations and shortness of breath. His vital signs are within normal limits, and EKG reveals atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option A- Metoprolol: Atrial fibrillation is a common cardiac arrhythmia characterized by an irregularly irregular rhythm caused by disorganized atrial electrical activity. The goal of treatment is to restore sinus rhythm or control the ventricular response to improve symptoms and prevent complications. Beta-blockers are the first-line agents for rate control in patients with atrial fibrillation and hypertension. Metoprolol is a selective beta-1 blocker that reduces the heart rate, decreases myocardial oxygen demand, and improves left ventricular function. The initial dose of metoprolol is 5 mg IV over 2 minutes, followed by additional doses of 5-10 mg every 5-10 minutes to achieve a heart rate of less than 110 beats per minute. Once the heart rate is controlled, the patient can be evaluated for anticoagulation and further management. Incorrect Options: Option B- Adenosine: Adenosine is used for the acute termination of supraventricular tachycardia. However, it is not effective for controlling atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. Therefore, administering adenosine is not appropriate in this case Option C- Synchronized cardioversion: Synchronized cardioversion is reserved for hemodynamically unstable patients with atrial fibrillation and a rapid ventricular response who fail to respond to medical therapy or who have signs of end-organ dysfunction. It is not the first-line option in a stable patient like in this case. Option D- Observe and reassess in 24 hours: Observing the patient and reassessing in 24 hours is not recommended as it can lead to worsening symptoms and complications in high-risk patients. Rate control or rhythm control should be initiated promptly, and further management should be tailored to the patient's individual risk factors and comorbidities. @Neet_pg_bot

Incorrect Options: Option B- Absent x descent: “x” descent is a drop in JVP due to relaxation of the right atrium. questions.solution: Correct Option B- Hypokalemia: The ECG above shows flattened T-waves, S-T segment depression and U-waves characteristic of hypokalemia . The potassium levels are important for myocardial depolarisation and repolarisation. Hypokalemia results in cardiac conduction abnormalities. When serum potassium levels fall below 2.7mmol/L, dynamic ECG changes occur. These include: T-wave changes (flattening and inversion) Tall P-waves S-T segment depression Prolonged QT interval Prominent J waves U-waves (a positive deflection after the T-wave best seen in V1-V4 leads) In extreme cases of hypokalemia, U-waves may become large enough to merge and cover the small preceding T-waves. Incorrect Options: Option A- Hyperkalemia: The ECG changes that occur due to hyperkalemia include: Peaked T-wave Loss of P-wave Prolonged PR interval S-T segment depression Widened QRS complex. It is not associated with a U-wave. Option C- Hypercalcemia: The ECG changes due to hypercalcemia include: S-T segment elevation Biphasic T-waves Shortened QT interval. It is not associated with a U-wave. Option D- Hypocalcemia: The characteristic ECG finding of hypocalcemia is prolonged QT interval . It is due to prolongation of S-T segment . questions.stem: A 36-year-old male presents to the clinic with a complaint of severe shortness of breath. The patient never smoked and is also seeking treatment with a hepatologist for liver issues. On examination, a prolonged wheeze is appreciated. Spirometry is performed and forced expiratory volume in the first second after the bronchodilator is 65% of the predictive value. A clinical diagnosis of emphysema is made. The patient inquires about the cause of the disease at this young age. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.stemHtml: A 36-year-old male presents to the clinic with a complaint of severe shortness of breath. The patient never smoked and is also seeking treatment with a hepatologist for liver issues. On examination, a prolonged wheeze is appreciated. Spirometry is performed and forced expiratory volume in the first second after the bronchodilator is 65% of the predictive value. A clinical diagnosis of emphysema is made. The patient inquires about the cause of the disease at this young age. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency Alpha-1 antitrypsin is a protease inhibitor which is synthesised by the liver. It inactivates the neutrophil elastase and protects the lung tissue. It is caused by a genetic mutation which causes a conformational change in the structure of alpha-1 antitrypsin. The dysfunctional protein affects the liver by accumulating in the hepatocytes' endoplasmic reticulum resulting in hepatitis and liver cirrhosis. In the lungs, its deficiency results in an uninhibited activity of neutrophil elastase, which causes pulmonary parenchyma destruction and results in pan acinar emphysema. Patients are < 60 years of age. Incorrect Options: Option B - Smoking Nicotine and smoking cause the inactivation of protease inhibitors and form reactive oxygen species. Smoking results in the destruction of respiratory bronchioles, resulting in centrilobular emphysema. Option C - Bullae formation In giant bullous emphysema, large bullae are formed, which cause the destruction of surrounding pulmonary tissue. Option D - Scar formation The chronic inflammation results in scar formation due to quartz exposure which results in cicatricial emphysema. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Perform tube thoracostomy in left third intercostal space: In pregnant women with a gravid uterus and an indication for a tube thoracostomy, efforts should be made to prevent diaphragmatic or abdominal entry during the procedure. Entering the thoracic cavity at a space higher than usual is indicated in this patient population. Incorrect Options: Option A - Perform emergent C-section: A perimortem C-section may be performed within 5 minutes of maternal cardiopulmonary arrest when the fetus is viable. There are 2 reasons why a C-section should not be performed in this case. First, the mother is not in cardiopulmonary arrest. Second, the fetus is estimated to be at 20 weeks gestation, which is not likely to be a viable pregnancy if C-section is performed. Option B - Tube thoracostomy is contraindicated: This patient has an indication for a tube thoracostomy (chest tube) given her injuries. She has multiple rib fractures with a large pneumohemothorax. The hemopneumothorax must be addressed before moving on to the other portions of trauma evaluation and resuscitation. questions.stem: A 55-year-old female is brought to an emergency department with substernal chest pain and severe dyspnea. The pain radiates to her left arm. Her blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg, her heart rate is 65/min, and her oxygen saturation is 88%. ECG shows 2-mm-ST segment elevation in anterolateral leads. Which of the following is the best next step in the management of this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old female is brought to an emergency department with substernal chest pain and severe dyspnea. The pain radiates to her left arm. Her blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg, her heart rate is 65/min, and her oxygen saturation is 88%. ECG shows 2-mm-ST segment elevation in anterolateral leads. Which of the following is the best next step in the management of this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Oxygen supplementation: ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) is a type of heart attack due to complete obstruction of one of the major coronary arteries. The treatment aims to restore the blood supply to the heart and minimize the damage to the cardiac muscle. Management of the STEMI is time-dependent . The faster the treatment can be provided to the patient, the better the positive outcome can be expected. If the patient's oxygen saturation is abnormal (<90%), oxygen should be supplied first. Aspirin 325mg, P2Y12 inhibitor (e.g., clopidogrel), and atorvastatin should be given. Morphine should also be given to control pain. Incorrect Options: Option A - Alteplase: Fibrinolytic therapy can be performed in patients where PCI is impossible due to lack of time. It should be performed within 120 minutes. It involves giving fibrinolytic medication like alteplase (tPA) to resolve the clot and restore the blood flow. However, this patient should be given an oxygen supply first. Option C - Percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty: Percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty (PTCA) should be performed within 90 minutes. PTCA is performed by assessing the coronary circulation by inserting the catheter via the femoral or radial artery. A dye can be injected to identify the blockage of the artery. A balloon can be inflated to resolve the blockage of the artery. Afterwards, a stent can be placed that helps to keep the artery open and prevents another occlusion. However, this patient should be given an oxygen supply first. Option D - Coronary artery bypass surgery: Coronary artery bypass surgery (CABG) is conducted by utilizing the patient's veins from the legs or arteries from the chest to bypass the occluded areas and restore the blood supply to the heart muscle. It is indicated when there is a three-vessel coronary artery disease of more than 70% with or without left anterior descending artery involvement, a two-vessel disease with the involvement of LAD and one other major artery , or the left main disease is more than 50%. However, this patient should be given an oxygen supply first. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml:
A 27-year-old woman presents to the ER with new onset fatigue and bruising. She is found to have new cytopenia with :
Hb 8.8 g/dL
WBC 6000/uL
Platelet count 22,000/µL
Peripheral blood smear reveals a population of large atypical cells showing occasional Auer rods with large lobed nuclei and violet granules.
Peripheral blood flow cytometry reveals a population of cells positive for CD13, CD33, and CD56 and negative for CD34 and HLA-DR.
You are concerned for APL, immediately start ATRA and monitor and correct her coagulopathy with supportive plasma and blood products. FISH studies return negative for t(15;17). You suspect a possible "cryptic" or variant APL translocation and contact the cytogenetic and molecular labs to expedite further studies. Which of the following is the most common "cryptic" or variant APL translocation?
questions.solution: Correct Option - A t(11;17)(q23;q21.1) - PLZF-RARA: Approximately 98% of APL (Acute promyelocytic leukaemia) cases will have a classic t(15;17) chromosomal translocation typically detectable by FISH probe for PML/RARA fusion. Rarely, cases with otherwise classic APL phenotype will not demonstrate the classic t(15;17) and these are often referred to as "cryptic" or variant APL, officially known as AML with variant RARA translocation by the World Health Organization (WHO). The most commonly reported variant RARA translocation is t(11;17)(q23;q21.1) in which the RARA gene is fused to the gene encoding PLZF (promyelocytic leukaemia zinc finger). questions.stem: A 25-year-old patient presents with a history of sudden episodes of irresistible daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, and vivid dreams that occur immediately upon falling asleep. Polysomnography reveals rapid onset of REM sleep. Which of the following best describes the pathophysiology underlying this patient's symptoms?
questions.stemHtml: A 25-year-old patient presents with a history of sudden episodes of irresistible daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, and vivid dreams that occur immediately upon falling asleep. Polysomnography reveals rapid onset of REM sleep. Which of the following best describes the pathophysiology underlying this patient's symptoms?

options.label: D
options.text: Impaired dopamine release in the substantia nigra

questions.solution: Correct Option A- Decreased orexin (hypocretin) production: This patient's symptoms are suggestive of narcolepsy with cataplexy, a disorder characterized by sudden, brief episodes of loss of muscle tone (cataplexy) triggered by strong emotions, as well as excessive daytime sleepiness and rapid onset of REM sleep during daytime naps. The primary pathophysiological mechanism involves a deficiency of orexin (hypocretin), which is a neuropeptide produced by neurons in the hypothalamus. Orexin plays a crucial role in regulating wakefulness and maintaining muscle tone. In narcolepsy with cataplexy, there is a selective loss of orexin-producing neurons. Incorrect Options: Option B- Overactivity of the locus coeruleus: The locus coeruleus is involved in the regulation of arousal and wakefulness. Overactivity of the locus coeruleus is not implicated in narcolepsy; instead, the disorder is associated with a deficiency of orexin-producing neurons. Option C- Excessive production of adenosine: Adenosine is a neurotransmitter that promotes sleep and relaxation. Excessive production of adenosine would typically lead to increased sleepiness, but it is not the primary pathophysiological mechanism in narcolepsy. Option D- Impaired dopamine release in the substantia nigra: Impaired dopamine release in the substantia nigra is associated with Parkinson's disease, not narcolepsy. Narcolepsy is primarily linked to the deficiency of orexin (hypocretin) and its role in regulating wakefulness. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman presents complaining of excessive sleepiness. She is having trouble staying awake at work and recently fell asleep while driving and crashed into a mail box. During the workweek she goes to bed at 1 AM and wakes up at 6 AM. She is unable to go to bed earlier because she works from 8 to 5 and takes night-time college classes. She needs to be up by 6 AM during the week to get her 2 children ready for school. Most weekends she works a second job to supplement her income and needs to be up by 5 AM on those days. If she is off she will sleep from 10 PM until 7-8 AM when her children wake up in the morning. Which of the following statements is true regarding her presentation?

If she is off she will sleep from 10 PM until 7-8 AM when her children wake up in the morning. Which of the following statements is true regarding her presentation?

options.label: A
options.text: She is suffering from behaviorally-induced chronic sleep deprivation which can have long-term adverse consequences for her health.

options.label: B
options.text: She should be prescribed a stimulant medication to help her cope with her busy schedule.

options.label: C
options.text: Her daytime sleepiness means that she probably has a primary sleep disorder resulting in unrefreshing sleep such as obstructive sleep apnea.

options.label: D

questions.answerText: She is suffering from behaviorally-induced chronic sleep deprivation which can have long-term adverse consequences for her health.
questions.solution: Correct Option A - She is suffering from behaviorally-induced chronic sleep deprivation which can have long-term adverse consequences for her health: This patient is getting on average 5 hours of sleep during the week and is inconsistently sleeping longer on weekends. Her short sleep duration is a function of multiple demands on her time from work and other responsibilities. This is causing her to be excessively sleepy and can result in many health complications including an increased risk for cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, mood disorders and cognitive problems. Incorrect Options: Option B - She should be prescribed a stimulant medication to help her cope with her busy schedule: A stimulant medication may help reduce her risk of falling asleep during the day but without increasing her sleep time to meet her sleep needs she will continue to be at risk for health complications and have impaired daytime performance. The best approach in this case is for her adjust her schedule to allow for more sleep throughout the week. Option C - Her daytime sleepiness means that she probably has a primary sleep disorder resulting in unrefreshing sleep such as obstructive sleep apnea: Though she should be queried about symptoms of other sleep disorders such as sleep apnea her daytime sleepiness can be easily explained by her short sleep time. Option D - Getting 5-6 hours of sleep during the week is fine as long as she sleeps for at least 8 hours on weekend nights: A typical adult requires 7-8 hours of sleep per night. Increasing the amount of sleep on days off to help offset sleep deprivation during work days can be beneficial to some extent. However, 8 hours of sleep on weekends is unlikely to be enough to address this degree of sleep deprivation during the week. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 23-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a history of easy bruising and prolonged bleeding following minor cuts and dental procedures. His medical history is unremarkable, and there is no family history of bleeding disorders. Laboratory investigations reveal normal platelet counts and morphology. You suspect an inherited bleeding disorder and consider Glanzmann thrombasthenia in your differential diagnosis. Which of the following platelet function abnormalities is MOST likely to be associated with Glanzmann thrombasthenia in this patient?
questions.stemHtml:
A 23-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a history of easy bruising and prolonged bleeding following minor cuts and dental procedures. His medical history is unremarkable, and there is no family history of bleeding disorders. Laboratory investigations reveal normal platelet counts and morphology. You suspect an inherited bleeding disorder and consider Glanzmann thrombasthenia in your differential diagnosis.
Which of the following platelet function abnormalities is MOST likely to be associated with Glanzmann thrombasthenia in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Decreased platelet adhesion leading to inadequate clot formation

options.label: B
options.text: Impaired platelet aggregation resulting in prolonged bleeding times

options.label: D
options.text: Increased platelet lifespan leading to platelet hyperactivity

questions.answerText: Impaired platelet aggregation resulting in prolonged bleeding times
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Impaired platelet aggregation resulting in prolonged bleeding times: In this clinical scenario, the patient's symptoms of easy bruising and prolonged bleeding following minor cuts and dental procedures are suggestive of a bleeding disorder. Glanzmann thrombasthenia is a rare inherited bleeding disorder characterized by a defect in the platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa (GPIIb/IIIa) receptor complex. This receptor plays a crucial role in platelet aggregation, as it mediates the binding of fibrinogen and other adhesive molecules, facilitating platelet-to-platelet interactions. In Glanzmann thrombasthenia, this receptor is dysfunctional, leading to impaired platelet aggregation. Consequently, patients with this disorder often experience prolonged bleeding times and mucocutaneous bleeding, as seen in this patient. Incorrect Options: Option A - Decreased platelet adhesion leading to inadequate clot formation: Platelet adhesion is an initial step in primary hemostasis, but Glanzmann thrombasthenia primarily affects platelet aggregation rather than adhesion. Option C - Reduced platelet production causing thrombocytopenia: Glanzmann thrombasthenia is not associated with reduced platelet production. Platelet counts in affected individuals are typically normal. Option D - Increased platelet lifespan leading to platelet hyperactivity: Glanzmann thrombasthenia does not result in an increased platelet lifespan. Platelet lifespan is typically within the normal range for individuals with this disorder. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 75-year-old male presents with nausea, vomiting, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, and severe altered mental status. His past medical history is significant for frontotemporal lobe dementia, esophageal stenosis, prostatic hypertrophy, and metastatic melanoma in remission. A physical examination is significant for right upper quadrant abdominal pain with a positive Murphy's sign. The surgical team recommends a cholecystectomy; after the procedure, the patient develops a significant increase in mental confusion. Vitals are as follows: temperature 39℃, BP 190/85 mmHg, PR 101 beats per minute, and RR 23 breaths per minute. Laboratory results are significant for the following: Hemoglobin: 11.5 g/dL Leukocytes: 19,000 cells/µL Platelets: 100,000 cells/µL AST: 150 units/L ALT: 110 units/L Creatinine: 1.6 mg/dL The patient has difficulty breathing, chest pain, and blood-tinged sputum. A bedside chest X-ray is ordered, and a diagnosis of aspiration pneumonia is considered. The patient is placed on empiric antibiotic therapy with cefepime, levofloxacin, and metronidazole. Due to the difficulty of obtaining a sputum specimen for culture, a bronchoscopy is eventually performed, which is significant for the organism observed in the images below. Serological testing of the serum for fungal organisms is inconclusive. Of the organisms listed below, which is the most likely cause of this patient’s pathology?

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Blastomyces dermatitidis This patient has an unexpected clinical finding of Blastomyces dermatitidis from the specimens obtained during bronchoscopy, as the most likely finding would have been a bacterial infection due to aspiration pneumonia (hence the antibiotic prophylaxis pending microbiology results). The most common site of involvement with blastomycosis is the lungs, comprising 91% of cases. The diagnosis can be made quickly by viewing a broad-based budding yeast on tissue preparations, as shown on the GMS stain in image 2. Without identifying the organism on tissue samples, a culture can take about 2 weeks to yield an identification of the organism. Serology is not helpful in the diagnosis of blastomycosis, as the test is not reliable and there is cross-reactivity with other organisms, most commonly Histoplasmosis. Typically, severe Blastomyces infections such as this are managed with amphotericin B (lipid formulation). Incorrect Options: Option A - Histoplasmosis: Histoplasmosis does not display a broad-based budding yeast. Antigen testing is quite sensitive for urine, but serum antigen testing for Histoplasmosis is not reliable. Therapy is typically with oral itraconazole. Option C - Coccidioides immitis: Coccidioidomycosis has precise serological tests available, unlike blastomycosis. In addition, a broad-based budding yeast would not be present with coccidioidomycosis. The treatment of coccidioidomycosis is identical to the treatment of blastomycosis: 2 weeks of amphotericin B. Option D - Sporothrix schenckii: Sporothrix schenckii typically presents as an ulcerated skin lesion. The yeast would appear cigar-shaped rather than displaying broad-based budding. @Neet_pg_bot

Chest X-ray shows pulmonary edema with a normal size heart. He has a systolic murmur and S4 and is hypotensive. Which of the following is true regarding his condition?

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: Patient can be managed medically and does not require surgery

options.label: D

questions.answerText: Patient needs afterload reduction and inotropic support
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Patient needs afterload reduction and inotropic support: This patient needs afterload reduction and inotropic support. This patient is suffering from acute mitral valve regurgitation, as evidenced by his acute onset of shortness of breath and pulmonary edema. Acute mitral regurgitation is often a result of a ruptured papillary muscle secondary to ischemia. A systolic murmur and S4 are classic signs but may be difficult to hear in the ED. Definitive treatment is surgical management with afterload reduction to promote forward flow and inotropic support in preparation for surgery. Intravenous nitroprusside can be used to reduce MR, by reduction of systemic vascular resistance. The decrease in severity of MR increases forward cardiac output and diminishes pulmonary congestion. Vasodilator use is often limited by systemic hypotension. Dobutamine is an appropriate inotropic agent. An intra-aortic balloon pump is also an option. Incorrect Options: Option A - Patient needs preload reduction: This patient requires afterload reduction to promote forward flow. Reducing preload will not help and may actually harm this patient. Option C - Patient can be managed medically and does not require surgery: Patients with acute mitral valve regurgitation usually require surgical management. Option D - Patient should receive warfarin for anticoagulation: There is no need for acute anticoagulation, especially as these patients often require emergent surgical repair. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Failure to reduce the carbidopa/levodopa dose appropriately for lower protein intake while NPO for the procedure One serious condition that patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) are at risk for is Parkinsonism-Hyperpyrexia syndrome (PHS). This typically occurs in patients with Parkinsonism on dopaminergic replacement therapy in the setting of a systemic stressor (e.g., a surgery, as in this case), and is essentially identical to neuroleptic malignant syndrome. It results from a dopamine-depleted state in the central nervous system. The features include dysautonomia, fever, marked rigidity, and encephalopathy. When severe enough, patients can have elevated creatine kinase levels, renal failure, and deep vein thromboses. This is most commonly seen in patients who are subjected to an abrupt withdrawal of their dopaminergic therapy, such as when they are hospitalized for a procedure (in this case a PEG tube, a common procedure in patients with advanced PD). Other triggers include infections (e.g., urinary tract infections, pneumonia), dehydration (especially in advanced PD), and administration of dopamine receptor antagonists (like prochlorperazine). This can also happen if a deep brain stimulator is inadvertently turned off or malfunctions. The mainstay of treatment is supportive care and returning dopaminergic therapy if it is withdrawn. In severe cases, dantrolene may be necessary and it is not uncommon for these patients to require ICU-level care. A similar syndrome may present with the predominance of dyskinesias, the so-called dyskinesia-hyperpyrexia syndrome. This results from too much dopamine replacement, and is treated by gradual withdrawal of the dopaminergic agent. Choice (C) is the correct answer in this case, as it is the one option listed that would not account for this patient's PHS. Incorrect Options: Option A - Dehydration: Dehydration can lead to electrolyte imbalances and metabolic disturbances that could contribute to altered mental status and rigidity. Dehydration should be considered as a potential cause and corrected if present. Option B - Urinary Tract Infection: Infections, including urinary tract infections, can cause systemic inflammatory responses and contribute to altered mental status in older individuals. Infections should be evaluated for and treated appropriately. Option D - Administration of Prochlorperazine: Prochlorperazine is an antiemetic medication that belongs to the class of drugs known as dopamine receptor antagonists. These medications can block dopamine receptors and potentially worsen symptoms of Parkinson's disease, including rigidity and altered mental status. @Neet_pg_bot

The severity of hyponatremia in heart failure is related to the severity of cardiac dysfunction, with more severe heart failure resulting in a higher degree of hyponatremia. Laboratory investigations may show a low serum sodium level (<135 mEq/L) and low serum osmolality (<280 mOsm/kg). Urine osmolality is usually greater than 100 mOsm/kg, indicating that the kidneys are attempting to conserve water. Urine sodium levels may be variable , depending on the severity of heart failure and the use of diuretics. Imaging findings may include signs of congestive heart failure, such as pulmonary edema, pleural effusions, and ascites. Treatment options include diuretics, which can reduce extracellular fluid volume and improve cardiac output, and strategies to manage heart failures, such as ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, and aldosterone antagonists. In severe cases, fluid restriction or hypertonic saline may be necessary to correct hyponatremia. Incorrect Options: Option A - Hypovolemic hyponatremia: It occurs through a decrease in the amount of extracellular fluid, which raises the effective sodium concentration in the extracellular fluid and raises the serum sodium concentration. questions.solution: Correct Option D - Increased intrathoracic pressures compressing the vena cava and impairing venous return: The lack of breath sounds in conjunction with the ultrasound findings which describe a lack of pleural lung sliding make the diagnosis of pneumothorax highly likely. In a tension pneumothorax , air is forced into the pleural space during inspiration and is not expelled during expiration, causing increased intrapleural pressures . Clinically, tachycardia and hypoxia develop and late in the course hypotension will develop due to decreased venous return from collapse of the vena cava. The other vessels such as the aorta and the cardiac chambers are relatively muscular and are not as prone to collapse or compression. On examination, there will be jugular venous distension as well as displacement of the trachea to the opposite side of the defect. This should be treated immediately, even if only suspected, as it can lead to cardiac arrest. If extra team members are present, ultrasound is highly sensitive in the confirmation of pneumothorax. Treatment for a tension pneumothorax is immediate evacuation of the intrapleural air with needle decompression and eventual tube thoracostomy. Incorrect Options: Option A - Compression of cardiac chambers: The heart is compressed long after the IVC is collapsed. Option B - Aortic outflow obstruction: Aortic outflow would be preserved much longer than IVC diameter. Option C - Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction: This is not likely given the presentation of chest wall trauma and absent breath sounds. @Neet_pg_bot

It is also used as a severity score to predict mortality due to community-acquired pneumonia (CAP). It consists of 5 variables; each scored 1 point. Patients with a score of 0-1 can be treated as outpatients. Patients with a score of 2 require hospital-supervised treatment. It can be a short-stay inpatient or hospital-supervised outpatient treatment. Patients with a score of 3 or more should be managed for severe pneumonia in the hospital. Patients with a score of 4 and 5 require intensive care treatment. questions.stemHtml: An 8-year-old boy presents with wrist pain after a fall on his outstretched right hand. A radiograph of the injury is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- Salter-Harris IV: The growth plate or physis differs anatomically in children and adults. Long bones in children are composed of the following: Diaphysis or shaft Metaphysics, or flared portion of the bone Physis or growth plate Epiphysis, which is the secondary ossification center. The longitudinal growth of long bones occurs primarily at the growth plate and disruption can result in asymmetry or deformity in children. The Salter-Harris classification is used to describe pediatric long-bone fractures near the physis. The radiograph shown above demonstrates a Salter-Harris IV fracture of the distal radius . Type IV is a combination of types II and III. In this case, the epiphyseal component of the fracture is the obvious lucent fracture line, and the metaphyseal component is a more subtle fracture laterally. Incorrect Options: Option A- Salter-Harris I: Type I fractures go through the physis only. Types I and V may be invisible on initial plain films. Option B- Salter-Harris II: Type II, the most common fracture type, extends from the metaphysis into the physis. It does not reach the epiphysis. Option C- Salter-Harris IV: Type III extends through the epiphysis and physis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 55-year-old male with a history of pneumonia is admitted to the hospital with severe acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Despite initial supportive measures, the patient's hypoxemia persists. Which of the following pharmacologic interventions has been shown to improve mortality in ARDS?
questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old male with a history of pneumonia is admitted to the hospital with severe acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Despite initial supportive measures, the patient's hypoxemia persists. Which of the following pharmacologic interventions has been shown to improve mortality in ARDS?
questions.solution: Correct Option C- Inhaled nitric oxide: In patients with severe ARDS, inhaled nitric oxide (iNO) has been shown to improve oxygenation by selectively dilating pulmonary vasculature, thereby improving ventilation-perfusion matching. However, it's important to note that while iNO improves oxygenation, its impact on mortality in ARDS is not consistently demonstrated in all studies. It is generally reserved for cases with persistent hypoxemia despite other supportive measures. Incorrect Options: Option A- Inhaled corticosteroids: Inhaled corticosteroids have not been proven to improve mortality in ARDS. Systemic corticosteroids are sometimes used in certain cases but are not the first-line treatment for ARDS and may have variable effects on outcomes. Option B- High-dose systemic corticosteroids: High-dose systemic corticosteroids have not shown consistent mortality benefits in ARDS and may be associated with adverse effects. They are not recommended as routine therapy in ARDS. Option D- Intravenous vitamin C: While some studies have suggested potential benefits of intravenous vitamin C in ARDS, evidence is not robust, and its routine use is not well-established. questions.solution: Correct Option A- Raynaud’s phenomenon: Recurrent vasospasm of the fingers and toes , typically in reaction to stress or exposure to cold, is Raynaud's phenomenon. It can happen independently of another illness (Raynaud disease) or in conjunction with it (usually autoimmune). Avoiding triggers, such as cold temperatures, nicotine use, and some medicines, is the main component of management. (e.g., CCBs, iloprost). This patient most likely has vasospastic angina, linked with other vasospastic disorders such as the Raynaud’s phenomenon. questions.stem: Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) has been used in the treatment of neurological conditions including multiple sclerosis and infantile spasms. When it was first approved for treatment of MS relapses, the benefits of ACTH were attributed largely to its corticotropism, however, since then it is clear that other mechanisms are important to its effect. Which of the following mechanisms contribute to the immunomodulatory properties of ACTH?
questions.stemHtml: Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) has been used in the treatment of neurological conditions including multiple sclerosis and infantile spasms. When it was first approved for treatment of MS relapses, the benefits of ACTH were attributed largely to its corticotropism, however, since then it is clear that other mechanisms are important to its effect. Which of the following mechanisms contribute to the immunomodulatory properties of ACTH?

options.label: C
options.text: Depletion of T and B lymphocytes through its effect on CD52 surface antigen

options.label: D
options.text: Activation of central and peripheral melanocortin receptors

questions.answerText: Activation of central and peripheral melanocortin receptors
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Activation of central and peripheral melanocortin receptors: More recently, it has been shown that ACTH activates central and peripheral melanocortin receptors. Melanocortins inhibit immune system cells including macrophages peripherally and microglia in the central nervous system. ACTH acts via corticosteroid-independent melanocortin pathways to promote a down-modulating effect on immune-system cells and the cytokines they synthesize (option D is correct). Incorrect Options: Option A - Modulation of sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor: Fingolimod is approved as a disease-modifying drug for MS. It is a sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) receptor modulator and is thought to work by trapping lymphocytes in the lymph nodes, thus preventing their egress into the circulation. Option B - Inhibition of dihydroorotate dehydrogenase: Teriflunomide, also used in the treatment of MS, selectively inhibits dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, a mitochondrial enzyme required for pyrimidine synthesis, which results in reduced proliferation of activated T and B cells. Option C - Depletion of T and B lymphocytes through its effect on CD52 surface antigen: Alemtuzumab, which can be used in the treatment of aggressive forms of MS, binds to CD52 present in T and B lymphocytes and leads to depletion of lymphocytes. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C- Post-measles subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE): The described clinical scenario is suggestive of subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a rare and severe complication of measles virus infection. SSPE typically occurs several years after the initial measles infection and presents with progressive neurologic symptoms, myoclonic jerks, and cognitive decline. EEG findings often reveal characteristic periodic complexes. Option D- Measles-associated acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM): Measles-associated acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) is an acute demyelinating disorder that can occur after measles infection, but it presents acutely, not several years later, as described in the scenario. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child presents with recurrent throat infections and difficulty swallowing. Upon examination, the tonsils at the back of the throat appear enlarged. The patient's medical history indicates that they had frequent respiratory infections since early childhood. Further investigations reveal reduced IgA levels in the saliva. Which of the following secondary lymphoid organs is most likely to be involved in this patient's recurrent infections?
questions.stemHtml: A 7-year-old child presents with recurrent throat infections and difficulty swallowing. Upon examination, the tonsils at the back of the throat appear enlarged. The patient's medical history indicates that they had frequent respiratory infections since early childhood. Further investigations reveal reduced IgA levels in the saliva. Which of the following secondary lymphoid organs is most likely to be involved in this patient's recurrent infections?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Palatine tonsils: The palatine tonsils are a part of the lymphatic system and are located at the back of the throat. They are a type of secondary lymphoid organ that plays a crucial role in the immune response against pathogens entering the body through the respiratory and oral routes. Enlarged tonsils, as mentioned in the patient's case, can lead to recurrent throat infections and difficulty swallowing. Additionally, the reduced IgA levels in the saliva indicate a potential immune deficiency, which can contribute to the frequent infections. Therefore, the palatine tonsils are most likely to be involved in this patient's recurrent infections. Incorrect Options: Option A - Lymph nodes: Lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid organs that filter and trap antigens from the lymphatic system. They play a crucial role in the immune response by housing immune cells that help fight infections. However, they are not directly involved in the recurrent throat infections and difficulty swallowing described in the patient's case. Option B - Spleen: The spleen is another secondary lymphoid organ that filters blood and plays a role in removing damaged red blood cells and pathogens from circulation. It also helps initiate immune responses against blood-borne infections. While the spleen is important for immune function, it is not directly associated with the symptoms of recurrent throat infections and difficulty swallowing described in the patient's case. Option D - Thymus: The thymus is a primary lymphoid organ that plays a vital role in the development and maturation of T cells, which are important for cellular immune responses. However, the symptoms described in the patient's case are more indicative of issues related to secondary lymphoid organs, particularly the palatine tonsils, as discussed above. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 33-year-old female presents with a history of Budd-Chiari syndrome (diagnosed 4 years ago) and a portobiliary fistula (status post stents x2). She has a fever, hypotension, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain x1 day. The patient had an episode of nonbilious/unbloody vomiting. Jaundice is noticeable. She reports a fever to 104°F at home. After taking Tylenol, her fever went down to 101°F before she arrived at the hospital. She had 1 episode of periumbilical abdominal pain a few days ago, which resolved on its own. The patient and her family state that her jaundice has been improving. In the ED, the patient is tachycardic at 122 and hypotensive at 75/48. Her RR is 22, and her O2 sat is 99% on RA, but she is mentating and warm. Lactate is 7.6, and 1 L crystalloid was given by paramedics; an additional 2 L are administered in the ED with a continued BP in the 80s/40s. The patient's abdomen is distended and soft, with no ascites on ultrasound or focal tenderness. However, the patient complains of pain. She is started on Zosyn and vancomycin with 2 PIVs #18 and #16. After 2 L IVF, the patient is still hypotensive and is started on levophed. The GI physician recommends ERCP. The patient is transferred to the ICU while afebrile but tachycardic and hypotensive. She receives a total of 6 L crystalloid (including 2 L in the ED) with no significant change in BPs. Levophed is titrated up. The patient has no urine output, so a Foley catheter is placed. Meropenem, amikacin, and tigecycline (for antibiotic-resistant Enterobacter) are ordered. A stress dose of steroids is started. A central line and an arterial line are placed. She is intubated prior to ERCP. If a second vasopressor is needed for this patient's septic shock, what is the drug of choice?

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Vasopressin: Vasopressin levels in septic shock are reported to be lower than anticipated for a shock state. Low doses of vasopressin may prove effective in raising blood pressure in patients who are refractory to other vasopressors and may have other potential physiological benefits. Although guidelines suggest additional agents including vasopressin (up to 0.03 units/minute to reduce the dose of norepinephrine) or epinephrine (for refractory hypotension),practice varies. Vasopressin can be added to norepinephrine with the intent of raising MAP to target or decreasing the norepinephrine dosage. However, low-dose vasopressin is not recommended as the single initial vasopressor for the treatment of sepsis-induced hypotension, and vasopressin doses >0.03–0.04 U/min should be reserved for salvage therapy (after failing to achieve an adequate MAP with other vasopressor agents). Incorrect Options: Option B - Ephedrine: Ephedrine is a sympathomimetic drug that acts primarily on alpha- and beta-adrenergic receptors, similar to epinephrine. While it can increase blood pressure and heart rate, it is not the drug of choice for septic shock. Ephedrine is more commonly used as a bronchodilator and vasopressor in certain clinical situations, such as in anesthesia or hypotensive episodes due to spinal anesthesia. In septic shock, other vasopressors like norepinephrine and vasopressin are preferred due to their more specific effects on maintaining blood pressure and improving perfusion. Option C - Phenylephrine: Phenylephrine is a pure alpha-agonist that causes vasoconstriction, leading to an increase in blood pressure. While it can be effective in raising blood pressure, it is not the first-line choice for septic shock management. Phenylephrine is more commonly used in clinical settings where vasoconstriction is required, such as in certain types of shock, nasal decongestants, and pupil dilation during eye exams. In septic shock, the primary focus is on restoring vascular tone and maintaining organ perfusion, which is better achieved with vasopressors like norepinephrine and vasopressin. Option D - Renal-dose dopamine: In the past, dopamine was commonly used in low doses as a renal vasodilator to help improve renal blood flow and urine output in patients with acute renal failure or low urine output. However, current evidence does not support the routine use of low-dose dopamine for renal protection in critically ill patients, including those with septic shock. Instead, the focus in septic shock is on optimizing fluid resuscitation, adequate perfusion, and using appropriate vasopressors like norepinephrine and vasopressin to maintain blood pressure and organ function. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 4-month-old boy is brought to the paediatric outpatient department by his parents due to growth failure. The mother’s pregnancy was uneventful, and the boy was delivered by vaginal delivery at 37 weeks of gestation. Physical examination reveals a wide pulse pressure and a continuous machinery murmur in the left second intercostal space. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 4-month-old boy is brought to the paediatric outpatient department by his parents due to growth failure. The mother’s pregnancy was uneventful, and the boy was delivered by vaginal delivery at 37 weeks of gestation. Physical examination reveals a wide pulse pressure and a continuous machinery murmur in the left second intercostal space. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option A- Patent ductus arteriosus: The patient presents with the clinical features of Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). Ductus arteriosus shunts blood from the pulmonary artery to the aorta during foetal life and closes soon after birth. Failure to close causes left-to-right shunting of the blood from the aorta to the pulmonary artery after birth because pulmonary vascular resistance decreases after birth. PDA is associated with early pregnancy rubella infection. It can also occur in premature infants because of less responsiveness of the smooth muscles in the ductus arteriosus wall to high oxygen; therefore, it may not constrict after birth. Full-term infants with PDA have ductus arteriosus walls with deficient muscular media and mucoid endothelial layer, whereas the structure of PDA is normal in preterm infants. Spontaneous closure is common in preterm infants, but if PDA persists for longer than the first few weeks, it rarely closes spontaneously in full-term infants. Auscultation on the left second intercostal space will reveal a machine-like continuous murmur that may radiate to the left clavicle or sternal border. Although small PDAs are asymptomatic, heart failure occurs in large defects, and failure to grow can be a common feature in infants. Incorrect Options: Option B- Ventricular septal defect: Ventricular septal defect (VSD) is the most common congenital heart disease. It can occur in both membranous and muscular portions of the ventricular septum. A blowing holo-systolic murmur can be auscultated over the left lower sternal border. Excessive blood flow causes pulmonary hypertension, and large VSDs eventually lead to congestive heart failure. If ECG reveals right ventricular hypertrophy, pulmonary hypertension has developed, and the defect is large. As this patient did not have a holosystolic murmur, it is an unlikely diagnosis. Option C- Atrial septal defect: Ostium secundum atrial septal defect is the most common, and it occurs in the fossa ovalis. As most patients are, asymptomatic diagnosis is incidental in most cases, although intolerance to exercise may be present. On the left sternal border, the right ventricular heave may be palpated, and on auscultation, the second heart sound is fixed, split, and wide in all phases of respiration. As these findings were absent in this patient, it is an unlikely diagnosis. Option D- Tricuspid atresia: In Tricuspid atresia, there is no passage of blood from the right atrium to the right ventricle due to the absence of the tricuspid valve. The blood enters the left atrium through an atrial septal defect or foramen ovale. If great vessels are normally related, blood from the left ventricle through the aorta enters the systemic circulation and mostly flows through VSD to the right ventricle. If it is associated with transposition of great vessels, blood from the left ventricle enters the pulmonary artery. For blood to reach the systemic circulation, it has to traverse through VSD from the left to right ventricle. The murmur heard in Tricuspid atresia is a holosystolic murmur of VSD. questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to his pediatrician by his mother after she noticed “puffiness” of his face and neck for the past 7 days. Vitals signs are unremarkable, but physical examination reveals bilateral periorbital edema and bibasilar crackles. Serum analysis demonstrates hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia. Urine studies are pending. What is the best treatment of this child’s most likely condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 4-year-old boy is brought to his pediatrician by his mother after she noticed “puffiness” of his face and neck for the past 7 days. Vitals signs are unremarkable, but physical examination reveals bilateral periorbital edema and bibasilar crackles. Serum analysis demonstrates hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia. Urine studies are pending. What is the best treatment of this child’s most likely condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Oral prednisone: This patient likely has nephrotic syndrome. The most common condition in children resulting in nephrotic syndrome is minimal change disease (MCD). The International Study of Kidney Disease in Children showed that up to 77% of children presenting with idiopathic nephrotic syndrome developed this condition following minimal change disease. By comparison, nephrotic syndrome due to membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis occurred 8% and 7% of the time, respectively, in this population. In children, nephrotic syndrome primarily causes generalized edema. This often appears in the periorbital regions first, especially in the morning before gravity has had the chance to promote drainage. Some children develop signs of hypovolemia (e.g., tachycardia, decreased GFR) as the effective circulatory volume decreases and fluid is retained in the interstitial space. Hypertension and hematuria are rare in minimal change disease and are more likely in post-infectious glomerulonephritis and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis. As large amounts of protein are excreted in the urine, hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia occur. Hyperlipidemia may be a result of the liver’s response to falling albumin, as both albumin and lipid-related proteins are synthesized. Furthermore, immunoglobulins and coagulation factors may be excreted in the urine, possibly resulting in an immunocompromised state or thrombotic complications (often renal vein thrombosis or cerebral sinus venous thrombosis). The pathophysiology of minimal change disease is well studied. While light microscopy of renal biopsy specimens in this disease is often normal, electron microscopy reveals the effacement of the podocyte foot processes, which help form the glomerular filter. Since podocytes have a limited ability to regenerate, their destruction results in persistent glomerular damage. Furthermore, there may be an aspect of immune dysfunction that is critical to minimal change disease; the primary therapy for minimal change disease is oral prednisone, suggesting an autoimmune etiology. Incorrect Options: Option A - Symptomatic management: Treatment with a steroid is necessary. Symptomatic management is not appropriate. Option C - IV methylprednisolone: Treatment with oral prednisone is the usual approach, and intravenous steroids are not typically indicated. Option D - IV penicillin: The disease is not caused by an active infection, and antibiotics are not necessary. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 58-year-old male with a history of myocardial infarction 6 days ago presents to the emergency department complaining of shortness of breath and dizziness. The patient was walking around his neighborhood when these symptoms began 1 hour ago, preventing him from walking any further. His wife immediately took him to the hospital. Vital signs show a blood pressure of 80/54 mm Hg, a heart rate of 102 BPM, and an oxygen saturation of 89%. On physical examination, a soft, low-pitched, and decrescendo holosystolic murmur is heard loudest at the apex, and radiates to the axilla, but not elsewhere. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 58-year-old male with a history of myocardial infarction 6 days ago presents to the emergency department complaining of shortness of breath and dizziness. The patient was walking around his neighborhood when these symptoms began 1 hour ago, preventing him from walking any further. His wife immediately took him to the hospital. Vital signs show a blood pressure of 80/54 mm Hg, a heart rate of 102 BPM, and an oxygen saturation of 89%. On physical examination, a soft, low-pitched, and decrescendo holosystolic murmur is heard loudest at the apex, and radiates to the axilla, but not elsewhere. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Acute mitral regurgitation: This patient with a recent myocardial infarction (MI) presents to the emergency department in acute distress with shortness of breath and dizziness. His vital signs show hemodynamic instability and decreased oxygen saturation requiring urgent intervention. For a patient with a recent MI, the risk of various complications is greatly increased within the first week and is elevated for months afterward. During the first 3 days, the risks of arrhythmia and post-infarction fibrinous pericarditis are high. For days 3-7, the risks of interventricular septum rupture, posteromedial papillary muscle rupture, and ventricular free wall rupture are at their greatest. The acuity of this case (i.e., hypotension, decreased oxygen saturation due to pulmonary edema, and a holosystolic murmur) indicates possible posteromedial papillary muscle rupture, leading to acute mitral regurgitation. This requires immediate attention and urgent intervention. The murmur of acute MR may be early systolic, midsystolic, or holosystolic, as it is in this case. However, since the pressure within the left atrium markedly increases during ventricular systole and the pressure gradient between the left atrium and ventricle diminishes by the end of systole, the systolic murmur is most commonly a soft, low-pitched, and decrescendo murmur which often endswell before A2. Treatment of this condition involves a rapid decrease in cardiac afterload via nitrates, sodium nitroprusside, diuretics, or intra-aortic balloon pump counterpulsatio n. The anteromedial papillary muscle is less likely to rupture due to its dual blood supply from the left anterior descending artery and the left circumflex artery, whereas the posteromedial papillary muscle receives blood from only the posterior descending artery (PDA), which was probably the vessel occluded during this patient’s MI 6 days ago. Incorrect Options: Option A - Interventricular septum rupture: Interventricular septum rupture may arise as a complication 3-7 days after MI. The murmur is most commonly heard over the entire precordium. In addition, a thrill may be felt in some patients. There is sometimes a loud pulmonic component of the second heart sound, or tricuspid regurgitation due to increased right heart flow Option B - Ventricular free wall rupture: Ventricular free wall rupture is a catastrophic complication resulting in pericardial tamponade and hemodynamic instability. Although this can occur within the same time frame as a posteromedial papillary muscle rupture, it is unlikely to cause a holosystolic murmur. Option C - Aneurysm formation with thrombus dislodgement: Aneurysm formation with further thrombus involvement is a rare finding in the first week after myocardial infarction. The “false” aneurysm that may form during this period can rupture rather than cause thrombus formation. The “true” aneurysm that may occur weeks to months after an MI has the potential of forming a thrombus. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 33-year-old female patient right-sided thyroid nodule, biopsy confirmed to be medullary thyroid cancer, with her USG revealing 2 neck nodes, presents to your OPD. The calcitonin level is 350 pg/mL. What is the next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 33-year-old female patient right-sided thyroid nodule, biopsy confirmed to be medullary thyroid cancer, with her USG revealing 2 neck nodes, presents to your OPD. The calcitonin level is 350 pg/mL. What is the next step in management?

options.label: B
options.text: Total thyroidectomy plus central LN dissection followed by bilateral radical neck dissection

options.label: C
options.text: Total thyroidectomy plus central LN dissection

options.label: D
options.text: Total thyroidectomy plus central LN dissection followed by I-131 therapy

questions.answerText: Total thyroidectomy plus central LN dissection followed by bilateral radical neck dissection
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Total thyroidectomy plus central LN dissection followed by bilateral radical neck dissection In the case of medullary thyroid cancer (MTC), the primary treatment is surgical removal of the thyroid gland (total thyroidectomy) because MTC arises from the parafollicular C cells within the thyroid. Additionally, central lymph node (LN) dissection is typically performed as part of the initial surgery because MTC often spreads to the nearby central lymph nodes. Incorrect Options: Option A - Radiation: Radiation therapy is generally not the primary treatment for MTC. Surgery, as described above, is the primary treatment, and radiation therapy may be considered in specific cases where the tumor is unresectable or there is residual disease after surgery. Option C - Total thyroidectomy plus central LN dissection: This option involves the removal of the thyroid gland and central lymph node dissection, which is appropriate for MTC. However, it does not address the potential need for radical neck dissection, especially in cases of elevated calcitonin levels or lymph node involvement, as mentioned earlier. Option D - Total thyroidectomy plus central LN dissection followed by I-131 therapy: I-131 therapy (radioactive iodine therapy) is typically used for differentiated thyroid cancers (e.g., papillary or follicular) that can concentrate iodine. MTC does not respond to I-131 therapy because it arises from different cells within the thyroid and does not have the same iodine uptake mechanism. Therefore, I-131 therapy is not the standard treatment for MTC. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B- Hyperkalemia: The ECG (in the question) show loss of P-waves, peaked T-waves and widened QRS complexes which are characteristic findings of hyperkalaemia. The potassium levels are important for myocardial depolarisation and repolarisation. The ECG changes that occur due to hyperkalaemia include: Peaked T-wave Loss of P-wave Prolonged PR interval S-T segment depression Widened QRS complex. Incorrect Options: Option A - Hypokalemia: When serum potassium levels fall below 2.7mmol/L, dynamic ECG changes occur. Other changes may include premature ventricular contraction, tachycardia, and Torsade de pointes. As these findings are absent in the above given ECG, it is less likely a cause. Option C- Hypocalcemia: The characteristic ECG finding of hypocalcemia is prolonged QT interval . It is due to prolongation of S-T segment . The degree of QT prolongation is directly proportional to the degree of hypocalcemia. As these findings are absent in the above given ECG, it is less likely a cause. questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the clinic by his parents with a palpable abdominal mass that does not cross the midline and hematuria. Which genetic mutation causes this condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the clinic by his parents with a palpable abdominal mass that does not cross the midline and hematuria. Which genetic mutation causes this condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option A- WT1 gene: Wilms tumour arises from the abnormal proliferation of metanephric blastema , the precursor to renal parenchyma. Wilms tumour is associated with genetic mutations, most commonly in the WT1 and WT2 genes located on chromosome 11. Clinical features of Wilms tumour include: Painless, palpable abdominal mass that does not cross the midline Hematuria Abdominal pain (less common) Hypertension Diagnosis: Abdominal ultrasound: Initial imaging modality to identify the mass. Hypervascular tumours with hypoechoic areas of necrosis is the ultrasound finding. Abdominal CT or MRI: Further assessment of the mass, involvement of surrounding structures, and staging. Chest X-ray or CT: Evaluation for pulmonary metastases. Treatment: Surgical resection: Nephrectomy or partial nephrectomy. Chemotherapy: Pre- or post-surgical treatment depending on the tumour stage. Radiation therapy: Used in advanced stages or high-risk cases. Incorrect Options: Option B- MEN1 gene: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1 (MEN1) is caused by the MEN1 gene mutation. MEN1 is characterised by tumours of the parathyroid glands, pituitary gland, and pancreatic islet cells. MEN1 is not typically associated with renal malignancies like Wilms tumour. Option C- BRCA1 gene: Mutations in the BRCA1 gene increase the risk of developing breast and ovarian cancers. BRCA1 gene mutations are not typically associated with renal malignancies like Wilms tumour. Option D- TP53 gene: Mutations in the TP53 gene are associated with Li-Fraumeni syndrome . questions.solution: Correct Option C- ACE inhibitors can be used in combination with potassium-sparing diuretics for the treatment of Bartter syndrome: Bartter syndrome is a rare inherited disorder that affects the kidneys and causes a deficiency of potassium and chloride ions in the body. His medical records reveal that he has a mutation in the gene encoding for epithelial sodium channel (ENaC). His serum potassium levels are found to be low. questions.solution: Correct Option A- Amiloride: The patient presents with clinical features and investigative findings of Liddle’s syndrome. Liddle’s syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition caused by gene mutations encoding the epithelial sodium channel in the collecting duct ( ENaC), which is responsible for active sodium and water reabsorption . These mutations modify the structure of these channels, making them more resistant to degradation. Pseudohyperaldosteronism develops as a result. Amiloride or triamterene , potassium-sparing diuretics that directly inhibit the collecting tubule sodium channels and can correct both hypertension and, if present, hypokalemia, are used to treat Liddle syndrome. Incorrect Options: Option B- Thiazide diuretics: Thiazide diuretic use results in hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, hypocalciuria, hypomagnesemia and hyperreninemic hyperaldosteronism. As thiazide diuretics cause hypokalemia, they are not used in the treatment of Liddle’s syndrome. Gitelman syndrome has a similar presentation to chronic thiazide diuretics use. Option C- Loop diuretics: Loop diuretic use results in hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, elevated renin and aldosterone, potassium and chloride excretion, low serum, and urine magnesium levels. As loop diuretics cause hypokalemia, they are not used in the treatment of Liddle’s syndrome. Barter syndrome presents similarly to chronic loop diuretics use . Option D- Corticosteroids: Corticosteroids such as prednisolone can cause hypernatremia, hypokalemia, and fluid retention, resulting in a similar presentation to Liddle’s syndrome. Hence, corticosteroids are not effective for Liddle’s syndrome. @Neet_pg_bot
